Agaricus augustus, commonly called The Prince, is a large, handsome member of the Agaricaceae and one of the choicest edible Agaricus species. The cap is robust (often 10-20 cm, sometimes larger) and densely covered with fine brownish to golden-brown fibrillose scales over a pale ground, giving an overall tan to ochre-brown appearance; it expands from hemispherical to broadly convex or nearly flat. The crowded gills begin pale pinkish-grey and mature through pink to a deep chocolate-brown, never remaining white. The stout stem bears a large, conspicuous, pendant white ring and the surface below the ring is often somewhat shaggy or scaly. The flesh is firm and white and may slowly stain a faint yellow where handled, but does NOT flash bright chrome-yellow at the stem base. A defining feature is the strong, pleasant smell of almonds or marzipan (anise/benzaldehyde-like). The spore print is dark chocolate-brown. It is a saprotrophic, ground-dwelling fungus fruiting in summer and autumn, frequently near conifers, along paths, in woodland edges, hedgerows, gardens and disturbed ground across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, and introduced elsewhere.

Edibility and safety: The Prince is a highly regarded edible and should always be cooked thoroughly; never eaten raw. The single most important safety task is distinguishing it from toxic, phenolic Agaricus species, above all the Yellow Stainer (Agaricus xanthodermus), which stains an instant, vivid chrome-yellow when the flesh is cut or scratched - most reliably at the very base of the stem - and smells unpleasant of phenol/ink/iodine rather than almond. These species cause gastrointestinal upset (cramping, vomiting, diarrhoea) in many people. Always cut the stem base to check for bright-yellow staining and confirm the almond odour before eating. As with any pale or partly white mushroom, beginners must also rule out deadly white Amanita species, which differ by having a WHITE spore print, free white gills that never turn brown, and a membranous sac-like volva at the swollen stem base - features never present in Agaricus. When in doubt, do not eat. Some foragers report mild gastrointestinal sensitivity to large quantities even of correctly identified Agaricus, and individual reactions vary, so try a small portion first.
edibilityNotes: Choice edible but must be cooked, never eaten raw. Critical: cut the stem base and reject any specimen that flashes bright chrome-yellow (Yellow Stainer A. xanthodermus and other phenolic Agaricus such as A. moelleri, toxic) or that smells of phenol/ink rather than almonds. Rule out deadly white Amanita (white spore print + sac-like volva). Eat a small portion first; individual sensitivity varies.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere (Europe, North America, Asia, North Africa) and introduced to other temperate areas.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus xanthodermus
dangerousLookalikes.note: The Yellow Stainer (toxic). Stains an instant bright chrome-yellow when cut, most strongly at the stem base, and smells of phenol/ink/iodine rather than almonds. Causes gastrointestinal illness. This is the key dangerous confusion.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus moelleri
dangerousLookalikes.note: Inky / Dark-scaled Mushroom (toxic; also known as A. praeclaresquamosus). Greyish fibrillose-scaly cap, stains chrome-yellow especially at the stem base, and has an unpleasant phenolic/ink odour rather than almonds. Causes gastrointestinal upset like the Yellow Stainer.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita (deadly white species)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Deadly white Amanitas (e.g. Destroying Angel, Amanita virosa/bisporigera) can be confused with any pale Agaricus. They have a WHITE spore print, free gills that stay white (never turning pink then chocolate-brown), and a membranous sac-like volva at the swollen stem base. Always check spore-print colour and excavate the stem base.

Agaricus bisporus is the cultivated supermarket mushroom, sold immature and white as the "button" or brown as the "cremini," and at full maturity as the "portobello." It is the most widely cultivated and economically important mushroom in the world, grown commercially on pasteurized composted substrate.
edibilityNotes: Choice edible and one of the most consumed mushrooms globally, but should be cooked before eating. Raw and undercooked fruiting bodies contain the naturally occurring hydrazine derivative agaritine; thorough cooking reduces agaritine levels and improves digestibility. Caution for foragers: never eat a wild white Agaricus-like mushroom without taking a spore print (must be dark/chocolate-brown, NOT white) and digging up the entire stem base to rule out a deadly Amanita.
distribution: Found in grasslands and manured/disturbed soils across Europe, North America, and other temperate regions; now cultivated and consumed worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides (Death Cap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Deadly. Has WHITE gills that stay white at all ages and a WHITE spore print, plus a membranous ring and a sac-like volva at the swollen stem base. Agaricus bisporus has pink-to-chocolate-brown gills, a dark brown spore print, and no volva.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita virosa / Destroying Angel
dangerousLookalikes.note: Deadly. Entirely white with white gills, white spore print, a ring, and a volva at the base. Always check spore print color and dig up the whole stem base before eating any white Agaricus-like mushroom.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus xanthodermus (Yellow Stainer)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic, causes gastrointestinal upset in most people. Bruises bright chrome yellow (especially at the stem base when cut) and has a phenolic/ink-like or carbolic smell, versus the pleasant mushroomy smell of A. bisporus.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Leucoagaricus leucothites (White Dapperling)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Pinkish-white to white gills and a WHITE spore print (vs. the dark brown print of A. bisporus); can be confused with white button forms. Some white-gilled lookalikes are toxic, so a spore print is essential.

Agaricus campestris, the field or meadow mushroom, is a common edible agaric of grasslands worldwide. Its cap is white, the gills are bright pink when young and mature through red to chocolate-brown, and it produces a dark brown spore print. It is closely related to the cultivated button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus).
edibilityNotes: A choice edible that should always be cooked before eating. The critical danger is misidentifying a young, button-stage destroying angel or death cap (Amanita) as a field mushroom: these are DEADLY due to amatoxins, which cause delayed gastrointestinal symptoms 6-24+ hours after the meal followed by apparent recovery and then fatal liver and kidney failure. Amanita species have WHITE gills that never turn pink or brown, a white spore print, and a membranous cup (volva) at a swollen base often hidden below the soil line. Always dig up the entire base to check for a volva, confirm pink-to-brown gills and a dark brown spore print, and avoid any all-white-gilled specimen. Also distinguish the toxic Agaricus xanthodermus (yellow stainer), which bruises chrome-yellow (most strongly at the stem base when cut) and smells unpleasantly phenolic/of ink or carbolic; A. campestris does not stain strongly yellow and smells pleasantly mushroomy. Note that pink-gilled buttons can resemble young Amanita whose gills have not yet been exposed, so spore print and volva checks are essential.
distribution: Widespread and common across temperate regions worldwide, including Europe, North America, and Asia, with introduced ranges elsewhere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Destroying angel / death cap (Amanita virosa, A. phalloides and allies)
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY (amatoxins; delayed-onset liver/kidney failure). Distinguished by white gills that never turn pink or brown, a white spore print, and a membranous cup (volva) at a swollen base; young button-stage specimens are the most dangerous because they superficially resemble a field mushroom. Field mushrooms have pink-to-brown gills, a dark brown spore print, and no volva.

Amanita caesarea, Caesar's Mushroom, is a large, striking agaric prized as a choice edible since Roman times (its Latin name references the Caesars). It produces a smooth, bright orange to orange-red cap (typically 8-15 cm, occasionally to 20 cm) that is hemispherical when young and expands to broadly convex or flat, usually with a faintly striate margin. Unlike most Amanita, the cap is smooth and generally free of the white universal-veil warts seen in the fly agaric. The free gills, stem, and ring are a distinctive lemon to golden yellow, and the white, sac-like, membranous volva (cup) enclosing the base is large and persistent. The young fruitbody emerges from a white "egg" of universal veil tissue. It is ectomycorrhizal, associating chiefly with oak (Quercus) and chestnut, fruiting in warm summer and autumn weather, and is native to southern Europe and parts of North Africa and western Asia; similar but distinct related taxa (e.g. A. jacksonii) occur in North America and Asia. CRITICAL SAFETY NOTE: A. caesarea can be confused by inexperienced foragers with the toxic fly agaric, Amanita muscaria, which has a red to orange cap studded WITH white warts and WHITE gills and stem. Because the genus Amanita also contains the world's deadliest mushrooms (the amatoxin-bearing death cap and destroying angels), no Amanita should ever be eaten without confident genus- and species-level identification by an expert. The combination of a smooth orange cap, yellow gills/stem/ring, and a white sac-like volva is the key diagnostic for A. caesarea.
distribution: Native to southern Europe (notably Italy, the Balkans, Iberia, southern France) and extending into North Africa and western Asia; favours warm, often Mediterranean climates. Historically reported more widely, but several similar populations in North America and Asia are now recognised as separate species (e.g. A. jacksonii).
edibilityNotes: A highly regarded choice edible, traditionally eaten cooked and sometimes the young "eggs" sliced raw in salads in parts of Italy. However, because of the severe danger of confusing any Amanita with deadly amatoxin-containing species (death cap, destroying angels) or with the toxic Amanita muscaria, only foragers with confident genus- and species-level expertise should ever consume it. Key field marks: smooth orange cap (no white warts), yellow free gills/stem/ring, white sac-like volva, white spore print.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita muscaria
dangerousLookalikes.note: Fly agaric: red to orange cap studded WITH white/cream warts, and WHITE gills, stem, and ring (not yellow). Toxic (ibotenic acid/muscimol), causing delirium and GI distress. The white warts and white gills are the decisive differences from the smooth-capped, yellow-gilled A. caesarea.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides
dangerousLookalikes.note: Death cap: DEADLY amatoxin mushroom with a greenish to olive or yellowish cap, WHITE gills, white stem with ring and a sac-like volva. Some pale-yellow forms could mislead. Causes delayed-onset (typically 6-24 h) symptoms followed by potentially fatal liver and kidney failure. No Amanita should be eaten without expert ID.

Distinguished from A. caesarea by warted cap, white (not yellow) gills, and lack of the smooth orange cap with persistent sac-like volva.

Amanita pantherina, the Panther Cap, is a toxic and psychoactive mushroom of Europe and Asia recognized by its brown cap dotted with white warts, a ring on the stem, and concentric hoop-like volval rings at the swollen base. It contains the isoxazole compounds ibotenic acid and muscimol — the same toxins as the fly agaric (A. muscaria) — typically at higher and more variable concentrations.
edibilityNotes: Toxic and psychoactive — not edible. Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, producing "pantherina syndrome": confusion, agitation, ataxia, delirium, drowsiness, and sometimes seizures or coma. Toxin levels are higher and more erratic than in A. muscaria, making poisoning more severe; fatalities are rare but reported. The principal real-world danger is mistaking the panther cap for the edible Blusher (Amanita rubescens) or for Amanita excelsa/spissa. It can also be confused with the fly agaric (A. muscaria), which shares the same toxins.
distribution: Widespread across Europe and Asia; closely related forms are reported in North America and elsewhere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita rubescens
dangerousLookalikes.note: The Blusher; edible only when thoroughly cooked. Flesh bruises and stains pinkish-red where cut or damaged, and it lacks the sharp concentric basal volval rings of A. pantherina. Foragers seeking the Blusher risk taking the toxic panther cap instead.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita excelsa
dangerousLookalikes.note: Grey-brown European species (and its variety spissa), considered edible by some. Distinguished by greyish warts, a grooved ring, and a stem base lacking the sharp hoop-like marginal volval rings of A. pantherina; flesh does not redden as in the Blusher.

The death cap is a deadly poisonous ectomycorrhizal mushroom responsible for the majority of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. It typically produces a greenish to yellowish cap, white free gills, a white skirt-like ring, and a membranous sac-like volva at the base, with a white spore print. Its lethal amatoxins cause severe liver and kidney failure, often after a deceptive symptom-free latency period.
edibilityNotes: Contains amatoxins (chiefly alpha-amanitin) that are not destroyed by cooking, drying, or freezing. As little as half a cap can be fatal to an adult. Symptoms typically begin 6-12 hours after ingestion (gastrointestinal phase), followed by a deceptive period of apparent recovery, then progressive liver and kidney failure. Seek emergency medical care immediately on any suspicion of ingestion. Never eat.
distribution: Native to Europe, it has spread widely via introduced trees and now occurs across North America, North Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of Asia and South America.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Volvariella volvacea (paddy-straw mushroom)
dangerousLookalikes.note: An edible species cultivated in Asia and a recurring cause of fatal confusion. Volvariella has a PINK spore print and pink mature gills, and lacks a ring on the stem; the death cap has a white spore print, white gills, and a distinct skirt-like ring. Both have a volva, so spore color and the ring are the decisive features.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita citrina (false death cap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Pale lemon-yellow, with a rounded marginate (not sac-like) volval bulb and a raw-potato smell; considered inedible but not deadly. Distinguished by the abrupt bulb versus the death cap's loose membranous sac-like volva.

Amanita rubescens, commonly known as The Blusher, is a medium to large agaric named for its diagnostic tendency to stain pinkish to reddish ("blush") where the flesh and surfaces are cut, bruised, or eaten by insects. The cap is 5-15 cm across, reddish-brown to pinkish-brown, often dusted with grayish, pinkish, or off-white wart-like patches (remnants of the universal veil). Gills are crowded, white, often becoming reddish-spotted with age. The stem bears a prominent pendulous, finely striate ring and swells into a bulbous base (without a free-rimmed sac-like volva), with veil remnants forming concentric ridges or warts on the bulb. The flesh is white, reddening on exposure, especially toward the stem base where it is frequently tunneled by larvae. It is a widespread ectomycorrhizal species of temperate Northern Hemisphere forests. The Blusher is edible only after thorough cooking: it contains a heat-labile hemolytic protein (hemolysin) that makes it toxic when raw or undercooked. Because it is an Amanita and closely resembles the toxic panther cap (Amanita pantherina), it is strictly an experts-only mushroom. Novices should never eat any Amanita.
edibilityNotes: Edible ONLY when thoroughly cooked. Raw or undercooked flesh contains a heat-labile hemolytic protein (hemolysin) that is toxic and, in quantity, can cause hemolysis/anemia; this toxin is destroyed by adequate heat. Strictly an experts-only mushroom because of its close resemblance to toxic Amanita species, above all the panther cap. Beginners should not eat any Amanita.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, common in Europe and Asia, and present in North America (though some North American material represents distinct, related taxa such as A. novinupta in the west).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita pantherina
dangerousLookalikes.note: The panther cap is toxic (isoxazole toxins ibotenic acid and muscimol). It has a brown cap with pure white warts, white flesh that does NOT redden when injured, a smooth (non- or only faintly striate) ring, and a basal bulb with one or two distinct free-rimmed hoop-like volval ridges. The absence of pink/red blushing when cut or bruised is the key separator from The Blusher; do not rely on a single feature.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita excelsa
dangerousLookalikes.note: The grey-spotted amanita (incl. var. spissa) is similar in stature with greyish warts and a striate ring, but its flesh does not redden/blush. Lack of the pink stain helps separate it from A. rubescens, though distinguishing it from the panther cap requires care.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita muscaria
dangerousLookalikes.note: The fly agaric is toxic (isoxazole toxins). Typically a brighter red to orange cap with white warts and white flesh that does not blush; colour and non-reddening flesh separate it from the dull reddish-brown blusher.

Amanita virosa, the European Destroying Angel, is a pure-white woodland mushroom and one of the most poisonous fungi known. Like its relatives in the death-cap group it contains amatoxins that cause delayed, often fatal liver and kidney failure.
edibilityNotes: Deadly poisonous; contains amatoxins (alpha-amanitin and related cyclic peptides). DELAYED, CUMULATIVE ONSET: symptoms are dangerously delayed, typically appearing 6-24 hours after ingestion (gastrointestinal phase of vomiting and diarrhea), often followed by a deceptive 'false recovery' period of 1-2 days before progressive, potentially irreversible liver and kidney failure. By the time symptoms appear, toxin is already absorbed and liver damage may be underway. A single fruiting body can be lethal. No safe preparation exists: cooking, drying, freezing, or parboiling does NOT destroy the toxins. Seek emergency medical care immediately on any suspicion of ingestion, even if the person currently feels well.
distribution: Widespread across temperate and boreal Europe; closely allied destroying-angel taxa (e.g. A. bisporigera, A. ocreata in North America) occur in Asia and the Americas.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus species (white edible mushrooms, e.g. horse and field mushrooms)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible Agaricus species have pink-to-chocolate-brown gills that darken with age and a brown spore print, and lack a volva. Amanita virosa has persistent white (free) gills, a white spore print, and a distinctive sac-like basal volva. Always check the base of the stem for a volva.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Edible puffballs (immature button stage)
dangerousLookalikes.note: At the immature 'egg' stage the volva-enclosed Amanita button can resemble a small puffball. Cutting it vertically reveals the silhouette of a developing capped, gilled mushroom inside; a true puffball is uniformly solid white flesh throughout with no internal structure.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides (Death Cap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly amatoxin-containing Amanita, distinguished by its greenish to olive- or yellow-tinged cap, whereas A. virosa is pure white. Both are lethal, so this distinction matters only for identification, not for safety.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Volvariella / Volvopluteus species (volvate edible mushrooms)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some edible volvate species also have a basal volva, but they produce a PINK to salmon spore print and pinkish mature gills, versus the white gills and white spore print of A. virosa. A spore print is essential when a volva is present.

edibilityNotes: Edible ONLY when thoroughly cooked. Raw or undercooked specimens are toxic and commonly cause gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Even when fully cooked, a notable minority of people experience GI distress, so first-time eaters should try only a small, well-cooked portion and wait at least 24 hours before eating more. Discard the tough, fibrous stems and eat only the caps. CRITICAL: positively distinguish from the deadly amatoxin-containing Galerina marginata (rusty-brown spore print, ring, grows clustered on wood) and the toxic Hypholoma fasciculare (purple-brown spore print, bitter taste, sulphur-yellow gills), both of which also grow in clusters on wood. Always confirm a WHITE spore print before consuming.
description: Armillaria mellea, the Honey Fungus, is an aggressive parasitic and saprotrophic root-rot pathogen of trees and woody plants, and one of the most economically damaging forest and orchard pathogens worldwide. It fruits in dense, honey-colored to tawny-brown clusters at the base of living trunks, on stumps, and over buried roots, typically in autumn. Caps are 3-15 cm, convex becoming flattened, honey-yellow to reddish-brown, often with fine dark fibrillose scales concentrated toward the center; the flesh is white. Gills are whitish, becoming pinkish to rust-stained with age, attached to slightly decurrent. The stem bears a prominent persistent whitish to yellowish cottony ring. The spore print is white. Underground and beneath bark the fungus produces tough black shoestring-like rhizomorphs ("bootlaces") that spread infection from host to host, and its mycelium is bioluminescent, producing the faint green glow known as foxfire. It is edible only after thorough cooking; raw or undercooked material is toxic.
hosts: a wide range of woody trees and shrubs
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, North America, and Asia. The name Armillaria mellea has historically been applied broadly; molecular work has split the older "honey fungus" species complex into several distinct species, so some regional records may refer to closely related Armillaria taxa.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY. Contains amatoxins (the same class of toxins as the death cap). Also grows in clusters on wood. Distinguished by a rusty-brown to ochre spore print (vs. white in Armillaria), smaller size, smooth (non-scaly) brown to honey-brown cap, and a thinner stem. Confirming a white spore print is essential before eating any honey fungus.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hypholoma fasciculare
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic (severe GI upset). Sulphur Tuft. Clusters on stumps and wood. Distinguished by sulphur-yellow to greenish-yellow gills, a purple-brown to blackish spore print, intensely bitter taste, lack of a true ring, and absence of dark cap scales.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pholiota species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some Pholiota also cluster on wood with scaly caps and superficially resemble honey fungus; they typically have brown to rusty-brown spore prints rather than white, and many are slimy/viscid when moist.

Auricularia auricula-judae, commonly known as Wood Ear, Jelly Ear, or (historically) Jew's Ear, is a gelatinous, ear-shaped basidiomycete fungus that grows on dead and dying hardwood. The fruiting body is typically 3–8 cm across, reddish-brown to dark grey-brown, with a thin, rubbery-gelatinous texture and a finely velvety, sometimes wrinkled or vein-like outer surface that resembles a human ear. The inner (spore-bearing) surface is smoother and paler, often with folds and ridges. It is firm and elastic when fresh, shrivelling to a hard, dark, horny mass when dry and reviving when remoistened.

Classically associated with elder (Sambucus nigra) in Europe—the source of its old folk name—it also fruits on many other hardwoods including beech, ash, sycamore, and elm. It can be found year-round in mild, damp conditions but is most conspicuous in autumn, winter, and spring. As a wood-rotting saprotroph (occasionally weakly parasitic on living trees), it plays a role in decomposing dead hardwood.

The species is widely eaten and commercially cultivated in East Asian cuisine, where it (along with related Auricularia species sometimes sold as cloud ear) is prized more for its crunchy-gelatinous texture than for flavour, which is mild. It should always be cooked. It is generally regarded as easy to identify with no deadly lookalikes—other jelly fungi that might be confused with it are not dangerous. Note that wood ear contains compounds with anticoagulant (blood-thinning) and antiplatelet activity, so eating very large quantities, or eating it while on blood-thinning medication, before surgery, or with a bleeding disorder, warrants caution.
distribution: Widespread and common across temperate and subtropical regions worldwide, including Europe, Asia, and the Americas.
edibilityNotes: Edible and widely cultivated, especially in East Asian cuisine, where it is valued for its crunchy-gelatinous texture rather than flavour. Must be cooked; not eaten raw. Contains anticoagulant and antiplatelet compounds; large amounts may have a blood-thinning effect. Caution is advised for people on anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication (including daily aspirin), those with bleeding disorders, and before surgery.

dangerousLookalikes.note: A translucent brown gelatinous jelly fungus on dead wood that can resemble wood ear; not dangerous, but lacks the distinct ear shape and has a more brain-like/leafy form.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Exidia species (e.g. Exidia glandulosa, witch's butter)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Brown to black gelatinous fungi on dead wood; not toxic, but form irregular blobs or pads rather than a distinct ear and lack the velvety outer surface.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Auricularia mesenterica (tripe fungus)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A closely related gelatinous fungus on hardwood; not dangerous, but forms bracket-like flaps with a hairy, zoned grey upper surface rather than an ear shape.

Boletus edulis, the porcini or king bolete, is a large, choice edible mushroom with a brown, bun-shaped cap and a pored (rather than gilled) undersurface that is white when young and ages yellowish to olive. It has a stout, pale tan stalk bearing a fine white reticulum (net pattern) near the top, and white flesh that does not stain blue when cut.
distribution: Widespread across the cooler temperate and boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere in Europe, Asia, and North America, and introduced with host trees to parts of the Southern Hemisphere including southern Africa, Australia, and New Zealand.
edibilityNotes: A highly prized, choice edible, eaten fresh or dried; dried specimens develop a stronger aroma. Cook thoroughly before eating and never consume raw. Only collect if you can confidently distinguish it from inedible bitter boletes (Tylopilus felleus, Caloboletus calopus) and from red-pored or blue-staining toxic boletes such as Rubroboletus satanas. Key positive features: white-to-olive pores (never red/orange), white non-blue-staining flesh, mild taste, and a fine white net on the upper stem.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Tylopilus felleus (Bitter Bolete)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerously toxic but intensely bitter, ruining a dish. Has a coarse dark net on the stem, pink-tinted pores in age, and a pinkish-brown spore print, versus the white-to-olive pores and olive-brown spore print of B. edulis.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Caloboletus calopus (Bitter Beech Bolete)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Bitter and indigestible. Distinguished by a yellow, red-flushed stem, blue-staining flesh, and bitter taste; B. edulis flesh does not stain blue and tastes mild.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Rubroboletus satanas (Devil's Bolete)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic, causing severe gastrointestinal upset (especially raw). Has red to orange pores and blue-staining flesh, unlike the white-to-olive pores and non-staining flesh of B. edulis.

The Giant Puffball is a large, often soccer-ball-sized, smooth white spherical fungus that grows in meadows, pastures, and woodland edges. When young its interior is pure white and homogeneous, and it darkens to olive-brown as the powdery spore mass (gleba) matures. It is one of the largest fruiting bodies among fungi, sometimes reaching 50 cm or more across.
edibilityNotes: Edible only when young, with a firm, pure-white, completely homogeneous interior; it should be cooked. CRITICAL SAFETY: before eating ANY puffball, cut it vertically top to bottom. A true Giant Puffball shows uniform white flesh with no internal structure. If you see the silhouette of a developing capped, gilled mushroom inside, it is the egg/button stage of an Amanita (potentially the deadly Amanita phalloides, A. virosa, or A. ocreata) and must be discarded. If the cut interior shows any yellowing, gill-like patterning, or a tough/rooted central column, do not eat it. Once the interior begins to yellow, discolor, or turn olive-brown (spores maturing), it is no longer edible and may cause gastrointestinal upset.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including North America and Europe.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita button/egg stage (e.g. Amanita phalloides, A. virosa, A. ocreata)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Young egg-stage Amanita species can superficially resemble a small white puffball, but cutting them vertically reveals the silhouette of a developing cap, gills, and stem inside. Several of these Amanitas are deadly (amatoxin poisoning). Always slice every puffball top-to-bottom to confirm uniform, structureless white flesh.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pigskin / earthball (Scleroderma species)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Earthballs can look puffball-like but have a thick, firm rind and a flesh that is purplish-black to dark even when young (not pure white and homogeneous). They are toxic and cause gastrointestinal poisoning; the dark interior at the cut distinguishes them from an edible young Calvatia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Calvatia and Lycoperdon puffballs
dangerousLookalikes.note: Smaller true puffballs are also edible only when the interior is pure white and homogeneous; the same vertical-cut test applies to rule out Amanita buttons and to confirm immature, undiscolored gleba.

The golden chanterelle is a choice edible mushroom with a yellow-to-orange funnel-shaped cap and decurrent, blunt, fork-like ridges (false gills) running down a tapering stipe. It is ectomycorrhizal, fruiting from soil in association with trees, and is prized worldwide for its firm texture and faintly fruity (apricot-like) aroma.
edibilityNotes: A prized choice edible, but must always be cooked thoroughly; raw or undercooked chanterelles can cause gastrointestinal upset. Only eat after positively distinguishing from the toxic jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus) and the false chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis) by confirming the blunt, fork-like false gills (ridges), not true sharp-edged gills.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, North America, and parts of Asia. Note: many regional populations once called C. cibarius are now recognized as distinct species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus olearius (jack-o'-lantern)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic. Has true, sharp-edged gills (not blunt ridges), grows in dense clusters on wood or buried roots rather than singly from soil, and is more uniformly orange. Causes severe GI illness (muscarine-like / illudin toxins).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca (false chanterelle)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Has true, thin, repeatedly forked gills that are more orange than the cap, a softer texture, and lacks the fruity aroma. Generally regarded as poor or mildly upsetting rather than a choice edible.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus illudens (eastern jack-o'-lantern)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic North American counterpart. True gills, clustered on wood, contains illudin S; gills are bioluminescent in fresh specimens. Causes severe GI illness.

Chlorophyllum molybdites, the green-spored parasol, is a large white lawn mushroom whose mature gills and spore print turn dull green. It is the most commonly ingested poisonous mushroom in North America, causing severe gastrointestinal illness, which has earned it the nickname "the vomiter."
edibilityNotes: Toxic, causing severe but generally non-fatal gastrointestinal illness (violent vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps) typically beginning 1-3 hours after ingestion. It does NOT contain amatoxins or other delayed-onset deadly toxins; however, dehydration can become dangerous, especially in children and the elderly, and severe cases may require hospitalization for fluids. The toxin is not reliably destroyed by cooking. The single most reliable safeguard is the green spore print at maturity, which no edible parasol shares.
distribution: Widespread in warm temperate, subtropical, and tropical regions worldwide, and common across the southern and eastern United States, often fruiting in fairy rings on lawns after rain.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Macrolepiota procera (parasol mushroom)
dangerousLookalikes.note: An edible parasol; distinguished by a WHITE (not green) spore print, snakeskin-patterned scaly stem, and typically taller, more slender stature. Always check the spore print before eating any parasol.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chlorophyllum rhacodes (shaggy parasol)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Generally edible (can cause GI upset in some people), with a white spore print and flesh that bruises reddish/orange when cut; C. molybdites has a green spore print and lacks the same strong reddish staining.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chlorophyllum brunneum (shaggy parasol)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible relative with a white spore print and a thick, abrupt basal bulb; separated from C. molybdites by spore color (white vs green).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Leucoagaricus/Leucocoprinus and other white-spored parasols
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several smaller edible white-spored lepiotoid mushrooms can resemble young C. molybdites before its gills green up; rely on a mature green spore print rather than cap appearance.

Conocybe filaris (now generally treated as a synonym of Pholiotina rugosa / Pholiotina filaris) is a small, deadly poisonous "little brown mushroom" (LBM) widespread in lawns, gardens, and grassy or mossy ground. It is one of the few amatoxin-containing mushrooms outside the genus Amanita: it produces cyclopeptide amatoxins (alpha-amanitin and related compounds) of the same class found in the death cap (Amanita phalloides). The fruit body is small and unassuming — a conic to convex, ochre-brown to cinnamon-brown cap a few centimeters across, often somewhat wrinkled or rugose, on a slender stem. A key field feature is the persistent membranous ring (annulus) on the stalk, which is often movable and may be striate above; the ring frequently becomes dusted rust-brown by falling spores. The gills mature to rusty cinnamon-brown, and the spore print is rust-brown (a useful separator from white-spored Amanitas and from purple-brown-spored Psilocybe). Because it is small, brown, and grows in the same disturbed grassy habitats frequented by lawn mushrooms and by foragers seeking psilocybin species, it is dangerously easy to overlook or misidentify. Poisoning follows the classic amatoxin pattern: a deceptive latency of roughly 6–24 hours with no symptoms, then severe gastrointestinal illness, an apparent recovery phase, and progression to potentially fatal liver (and kidney) failure. There is no household preparation that renders it safe; cooking, drying, and parboiling do not destroy amatoxins. Any suspected ingestion is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospital evaluation.
edibilityNotes: Deadly poisonous. Contains amatoxins (alpha-amanitin and related cyclopeptides), the same class of toxins as the death cap. Poisoning is characterized by a delayed onset of symptoms (typically 6–24 hours after ingestion) followed by severe gastrointestinal distress and, after a deceptive remission, potentially fatal liver and kidney failure. Toxins are heat-stable and not removed by any cooking, drying, or parboiling. Suspected ingestion is a medical emergency — seek immediate hospital care; do not wait for symptoms.
distribution: Widespread in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including North America and Europe; reported from other temperate areas as well.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Psilocybe and other small brown psychoactive mushrooms
dangerousLookalikes.note: Foragers seeking psilocybin LBMs in grassy ground risk picking deadly Conocybe filaris; Psilocybe species give a dark purple-brown to purple-black spore print (not rust-brown) and often bruise bluish, whereas C. filaris has a rust-brown print and a persistent ring. This is the most dangerous confusion for this species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another small deadly amatoxin-containing LBM with a ring and rust-brown spores, but Galerina marginata typically grows on wood/conifer debris rather than in open lawns. Both are lethal — do not eat ringed, rusty-spored LBMs.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Conocybe and Pholiotina species (other lawn conecaps)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Numerous small brown lawn-dwelling conecaps look similar; many lack a ring or have not been confirmed safe. Reliable separation requires microscopy, and the genus is not a foraging target.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Panaeolus cyanescens
dangerousLookalikes.note: Confusable with Panaeolus cyanescens (psychoactive). See its profile for how to tell them apart.

edibilityNotes: Considered edible when young and thoroughly cooked, BUT it contains coprine, which produces a disulfiram-like (Antabuse) reaction when combined with alcohol. After eating this mushroom, consuming alcohol blocks acetaldehyde metabolism (the active metabolite inhibits acetaldehyde/aldehyde dehydrogenase), causing facial flushing/reddening, nausea, vomiting, malaise, palpitations, headache, and tingling in the limbs. Symptoms can begin within about 5-10 minutes of drinking and the sensitivity can persist for several days (reported up to roughly 3-5 days) after the meal. For this reason it is also called Tippler's Bane. DO NOT consume alcohol in the days surrounding a meal of this species. Only collect young, firm specimens before the gills begin to deliquesce (auto-digest) into black ink; old, blackening, liquefying caps are not suitable for the table. Many cautious foragers avoid this species entirely because of the alcohol interaction. Note: the coprine/alcohol reaction is associated with eating the cooked mushroom; there is no well-established separate 'raw toxicity' beyond the general rule to cook wild mushrooms thoroughly.
description: Coprinopsis atramentaria, the Common Inkcap or Tippler's Bane, is a widespread agaric that grows in dense clusters from buried wood, at the base of trees and stumps, and on disturbed or rich ground, in grassland, lawns, meadows, gardens, and along paths and roadsides. The egg-shaped to bell-shaped grey to grey-brown cap is often radially grooved or splitting, and expands and then liquefies (deliquesces) from the margin inward, the crowded gills auto-digesting into a black, inky fluid as the spores mature. The pale stem is hollow and fibrous. It is a saprotroph on dead and buried wood. Though edible when young and well cooked, it is best known for its coprine content, which produces a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
distribution: Widespread and common throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere (Europe, Asia, and North America), and also recorded in other regions such as South Africa and Australia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Coprinopsis variegata
dangerousLookalikes.note: A related inkcap with a cap covered in pale, felty veil patches/scales; also contains coprine and shares the alcohol interaction, so mistaking it does not change the safety advice.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Coprinellus micaceus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Mica Cap - smaller, more tawny/ochre cap dusted with glistening mica-like granules when young, growing in similar clustered habitats. A deliquescing inkcap that is easily confused; generally regarded as edible, though caution with alcohol is still advised when inkcaps cannot be told apart confidently.

Coprinus comatus is a common saprotrophic mushroom recognized by its tall, white, shaggy-scaled cylindrical cap that auto-digests (deliquesces) from the margin upward into a black inky liquid as it matures. It is widely regarded as a good edible when young and still white, but deteriorates rapidly after picking.
edibilityNotes: Considered a good edible when collected young, firm, and still white inside, with no black liquefaction; always cook before eating. The mushroom deliquesces quickly, dissolving into black ink within hours of picking, so it must be cooked soon after collection and old or blackening specimens discarded. There are anecdotal reports of mild gastrointestinal upset in some individuals, so try a small portion when eating it for the first time. Note: the alcohol/disulfiram-like (coprine) reaction is associated with Coprinopsis atramentaria, NOT C. comatus; correctly identified shaggy mane is generally regarded as safe with alcohol, but the practical danger is misidentification, so be certain of the ID.
distribution: Widespread and common throughout temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including North America, Europe, and Asia, and introduced elsewhere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Coprinopsis atramentaria
dangerousLookalikes.note: Common inkcap / tippler's bane. Smaller, smooth grey-brown cap lacking the tall shaggy white scales; typically clustered from buried wood rather than solitary in grass. Contains coprine and causes a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea, palpitations, headache) when consumed with alcohol, even up to a day or two later. Distinguish by the absence of shaggy upturned scales and the squatter, smoother, more bell-shaped grey cap.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chlorophyllum molybdites
dangerousLookalikes.note: Green-spored parasol, the most common cause of mushroom poisoning in North America. A young, unexpanded shaggy mane could be confused by a beginner with a young parasol, but C. molybdites has a brownish-scaled cap on a broader expanded form, a persistent ring on the stem, does NOT deliquesce into ink, and crucially yields a GREEN spore print (vs. C. comatus's black). Causes severe vomiting and diarrhea. Always take a spore print if unsure.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita species (young button stage)
dangerousLookalikes.note: In the very young 'button' stage, any white club-shaped mushroom emerging from grass or soil could superficially resemble an immature shaggy mane. Deadly Amanita buttons (e.g., destroying angels) have a universal veil/volva (sac or cup at the base), white gills and a white spore print, and do NOT have the tall shaggy scales or the black deliquescing flesh of C. comatus. Always slice young specimens lengthwise to check for an enclosed embryonic gilled mushroom and a basal volva; never eat unexpanded white buttons without confirming ID.

Cordyceps militaris is a bright orange, club-shaped entomopathogenic fungus that parasitizes the buried larvae and pupae of insects (notably moths and butterflies), erecting its fruitbody above the soil or leaf litter. It is widely cultivated on grain and other media as a source of the nucleoside cordycepin, and is distinct from the Himalayan Ophiocordyceps sinensis. It is used in medicinal contexts rather than as a culinary mushroom.
edibilityNotes: Not consumed as a food mushroom; the fruitbody is small and tough and is not eaten in the culinary sense. It is used medicinally as an extract, powder, tincture, or tea, and is not known to be toxic in normal preparations. It has no known deadly lookalikes: as a distinctive orange insect-parasitizing club it is unlikely to be confused with toxic gilled mushrooms. The main confusion is commercial/identity rather than safety, chiefly with Ophiocordyceps sinensis and other small orange Cordyceps species, which is an identification (not poisoning) concern. As with any fungus, do not forage and consume wild specimens without expert confirmation.
distribution: Cosmopolitan, occurring throughout North America, Europe, and Asia.

edibilityNotes: Deadly poisonous. Contains orellanine, a nephrotoxin that causes delayed kidney failure. Onset is dangerously deceptive: there are typically no or only minor early symptoms, with renal failure developing days to weeks (commonly 2-3 weeks, with a reported range of about 2 days to 3 weeks) after ingestion, by which time damage is often irreversible and may require dialysis or kidney transplant. Cooking, drying, and freezing do NOT destroy the toxin. Never eat any Cortinarius (webcap).
description: Cortinarius orellanus, the Fool's Webcap, is a deadly orange-brown webcap whose toxin orellanine causes severe, delayed kidney failure days to weeks after ingestion. The mushroom has a tawny to rusty orange-brown cap, widely spaced rusty-coloured gills, and a cortina (cobweb-like partial veil) typical of the genus. Because early symptoms are absent or mild, poisoning is frequently recognised only after irreversible renal damage has occurred.
distribution: Found in Europe, growing in deciduous woodland associated with broadleaf trees such as oak, beech, and birch.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible chanterelles are sometimes confused with the orange-brown cap; chanterelles have blunt false gills (forking ridges) running down the stem, no cortina, a pale to yellowish spore print, and a fruity apricot smell, whereas C. orellanus has true gills, a cobweb cortina, and a rusty-brown spore print.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Cortinarius rubellus (deadly webcap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly orellanine-containing webcap, similarly toxic; differs by its more conical/umbonate cap and association with conifers, but both are deadly and should be avoided.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Cortinarius (webcap) species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Many webcaps look broadly similar with rusty-brown spores and a cortina; because deadly orellanine-containers are nearly impossible to separate reliably in the field, no Cortinarius should be eaten.

edibilityNotes: DEADLY POISONOUS. Contains orellanine, a nephrotoxin that causes delayed-onset kidney failure. Symptoms are dangerously delayed: there are typically NO acute gastrointestinal symptoms in the usual hunting-and-eating window, and the first signs (thirst, frequent urination, headache, flank/kidney pain, nausea) often appear only ~2 days to 3 weeks after ingestion, by which time severe and frequently irreversible renal damage has occurred. Many victims have required dialysis or kidney transplantation. There is no specific antidote. Never consume any Cortinarius-type (cobweb-veiled) mushroom. Seek emergency medical care immediately if ingestion is suspected, even in the absence of symptoms.
description: Cortinarius rubellus, the Deadly Webcap, is a deadly poisonous mushroom of conifer and boggy woodland, formerly widely known under the name Cortinarius speciosissimus. It produces a conical to convex orange-brown to rusty tawny cap, often with a pointed central umbo, with a similarly colored stem and a fibrous cobweb-like partial veil (cortina) typical of the genus. The spore print is rusty brown. Its danger lies in the toxin orellanine, which damages the kidneys and produces a long, deceptive latency period between ingestion and the onset of symptoms. It has caused serious and fatal poisonings, including cases where foragers mistook it for edible mushrooms.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible chanterelles have been confused with webcaps in documented poisonings, but chanterelles have blunt forking false gills (ridges) running down the stem, a pale to egg-yellow color, a fruity apricot smell, a white/pale spore print, and no cobweb veil.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Cortinarius orellanus (Fool's Webcap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly orellanine-containing webcap with the same delayed kidney-failure syndrome; favors broadleaf woodland rather than the conifer/bog habitat of C. rubellus.

Craterellus cornucopioides, the black trumpet or horn of plenty, is a choice edible mushroom forming a dark grey to brownish-black, hollow trumpet- or funnel-shaped fruitbody. It lacks true gills, instead bearing a smooth to faintly wrinkled outer (hymenial) surface, and grows in troops on the ground in deciduous woodland.
edibilityNotes: A choice edible, highly regarded and especially prized when dried, which intensifies its aroma. Cook before eating as with most wild mushrooms. It has no known deadly lookalikes: the funnel shape, lack of true gills, and hollow trumpet body make it distinctive, though it is easily overlooked against dark leaf litter. As always, only eat foraged mushrooms identified with certainty.
distribution: Widespread across Europe, North America, and Asia, occurring in temperate hardwood forests of the Northern Hemisphere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Craterellus cinereus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Closely related and similar dark trumpet form; edible, not dangerous. Listed only because it can be confused with the black trumpet, not because it poses a toxicity risk.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pseudocraterellus undulatus
dangerousLookalikes.note: A smaller, similar greyish trumpet/chanterelle relative; edible, not dangerous. No deadly toxic species closely resembles the dark hollow trumpet form.

edibilityNotes: Toxic. Causes severe acute gastrointestinal poisoning (vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps), typically beginning 30 minutes to 2 hours after ingestion. Rarely fatal in otherwise healthy adults, but it is one of the more common causes of serious mushroom poisoning in Europe; severe dehydration and electrolyte loss can be dangerous for children, the elderly, and those with underlying conditions. The toxins are not fully characterized and are not destroyed by cooking. Never eat this species.
description: Entoloma sinuatum, the livid entoloma or livid pinkgill, is a large, robust mushroom of the family Entolomataceae with a pale grey-tan to ivory-buff cap. The cap is fleshy and broadly convex to flattened, often with a low umbo and a smooth, slightly silky surface, commonly 7-20 cm across. The gills are adnexed to sinuate (emarginate), starting pale yellowish or cream and maturing to a distinctive salmon-pink as the spores ripen. The stout, fibrous stipe is white and lacks a ring. The flesh has a mealy/farinaceous smell. A defining feature is the pink spore print, produced by the angular (polygonal) basidiospores typical of the genus. It fruits in summer and autumn, usually in deciduous (broadleaf) woodland favoring oak and beech, on heavy clay or calcareous soils. It is the type species of Entoloma and a leading cause of serious gastrointestinal mushroom poisoning across Europe, owing to its resemblance to several edible species.
distribution: Widespread across Europe; also reported in temperate North America and parts of Asia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Clitopilus prunulus (The Miller)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible but easily confused, and a frequent source of poisonings. The Miller is much smaller, with strongly decurrent gills (running down the stem), a strong mealy smell, and a pinkish (paler) spore print. Entoloma sinuatum is far larger with sinuate/adnexed gills that are not decurrent.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Calocybe gambosa (St George's Mushroom)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible. Fruits in spring (around St George's Day, late April), whereas E. sinuatum appears in summer/autumn. Calocybe gambosa has a WHITE spore print and crowded white gills, versus the pink gills and pink spore print of E. sinuatum.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus species (young button mushrooms)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Young Agaricus can resemble the pale cap. Agaricus has free gills that turn pink then chocolate-brown to blackish, a DARK BROWN spore print, and usually a ring on the stem. E. sinuatum gills stay salmon-pink, its spore print is pink (never brown), and it has no ring.

Flammulina velutipes, the velvet shank or enoki, is a cold-weather wood-rotting agaric with an orange-brown sticky cap and a distinctive dark, velvety stem. The wild form fruits in clusters on dead hardwood during late autumn and winter, while the cultivated form is blanched, slender, and long-stemmed from being grown in low light and high carbon dioxide.
edibilityNotes: A good edible that should always be cooked, and the tough stems are often discarded. CRITICAL: the wild winter form closely resembles the DEADLY Galerina marginata, which also grows in clusters on wood in cold weather and contains lethal amatoxins. The decisive separation is the spore print: Flammulina is WHITE, Galerina is RUST-BROWN, and Galerina also has a ring/ring zone on the stem. Never collect wild winter wood mushrooms without expert microscopic/spore-print confirmation; the safest source is cultivated enoki. Some people report mild gastric upset from undercooked or raw material.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, Asia, and North America.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY POISONOUS (amatoxins). Also clusters on wood in cold weather, but has a rust-brown spore print (vs. white in Flammulina), a ring or ring zone on the stem, and brownish gills. Flammulina has a white spore print, no ring, and a velvety dark stem base. Spore print is the decisive test.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hypholoma fasciculare
dangerousLookalikes.note: Sulphur tuft. Toxic (causes gastrointestinal illness). Clusters on wood like Flammulina, but is greenish-yellow with a purple-brown to olive spore print and intensely bitter taste; gills become green-tinged. Not deadly, but a common cluster-on-wood confusion.

authorship: (Bull.) B.K. Cui, M.L. Han & Y.C. Dai (2016); formerly Piptoporus betulinus (Bull.) P. Karst. (1881)
edibilityNotes: Not eaten as food: the flesh is tough, corky, and bitter. It has a long history of medicinal and practical use, typically prepared as a tea/decoction or extract rather than consumed as a vegetable. Young white flesh has been used traditionally as an antiseptic, styptic (to stop bleeding), and as a tinder/plaster/strop material. Modern interest centers on its bioactive compounds, but it should be treated as a medicinal/utility fungus, not a culinary one.
description: The Birch Polypore or Birch Bracket is a common bracket fungus that grows almost exclusively on birch (Betula). It forms smooth, rounded to hoof- or kidney-shaped brackets, usually 5-25 cm across, with a thin incurved margin. The upper surface is smooth and pale grey-brown to tan, often cracking with age, while the underside bears a white-to-pale-grey pore surface with small round pores. The flesh is white, thick, and corky-rubbery when young, becoming harder and bitter. It is a brown-rot fungus that acts as a parasite on weakened or stressed birches and continues as a saprotroph on dead wood, and it is one of the most frequent causes of death and decay in birch. Annual brackets typically appear in late summer and autumn but persist into winter. The species is famous for being among the fungal material carried by Otzi, the ~5,300-year-old Tyrolean Iceman, suggesting prehistoric medicinal or practical use. It has documented antiseptic, styptic, and anti-inflammatory traditional uses and is studied for bioactive triterpenoids.
distribution: Widespread throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, northern Asia, and North America, wherever birch trees grow.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Fomes fomentarius (Tinder Bracket)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Perennial, hard hoof-shaped grey bracket usually on birch or beech, but with a much harder, layered, woody body and a brown context; not the smooth pale annual bracket of the birch polypore. Not a poisoning risk, but commonly confused.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ganoderma applanatum (Artist's Bracket)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Perennial, flatter, woody bracket with a white pore surface that bruises brown when scratched; grows on various broadleaf trees rather than almost exclusively birch.

Galerina marginata is a small, rusty-brown, wood-rotting mushroom commonly known as the Funeral Bell or Deadly Galerina. It is a classic "little brown mushroom" (LBM) that fruits in clusters on decaying conifer and hardwood logs, and it contains the same amatoxins responsible for fatalities from the death cap (Amanita phalloides).
edibilityNotes: Deadly poisonous. Contains amatoxins (chiefly alpha- and beta-amanitin), heat-stable cyclopeptide toxins also found in the death cap. Onset is dangerously delayed and the course is biphasic: gastrointestinal distress (vomiting, watery diarrhea, cramping) typically begins about 6 to 24 hours after ingestion, often followed by a deceptive apparent recovery, then progressive liver and kidney failure that can be fatal. Cooking, drying, and freezing do NOT destroy the toxins, and there is no reliable field test. Never eat any small brown mushroom growing on wood without expert confirmation.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including North America, Europe, and Asia, with records also reported from Australia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Kuehneromyces mutabilis
dangerousLookalikes.note: The edible Sheathed Woodtuft also grows in clusters on dead wood and looks very similar. It is best separated by a scaly/scurfy lower stem below the ring, whereas Galerina marginata has a smoother, silky-fibrillose stem. Because the overlap is close and the consequence of error is death, beginners should avoid collecting either.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Psilocybe species (wood-rotting)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Wood-inhabiting Psilocybe sought for psilocybin grow in the same habitat and can superficially resemble Galerina; fatal misidentifications have occurred among foragers. Galerina has a rusty-brown spore print (Psilocybe spore prints are purple-brown to blackish-purple) and does not bruise blue, whereas blue bruising is common in psilocybin-active species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pholiota species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some small Pholiota also fruit in brownish wood clusters and can be confused among LBMs. Spore print color and microscopy separate them; they are not deadly but contribute to identification confusion.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hypholoma (Naematoloma) species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Wood-clustering Hypholoma such as H. fasciculare (Sulphur Tuft, toxic) and H. capnoides (edible) occur in the same logs and clusters; they typically have purple-brown to greenish-tinged spore deposits rather than the rusty-brown of Galerina, and a yellower or greenish cast to the gills/flesh.

Ganoderma lucidum, known as Reishi or Lingzhi, is a woody, shelf-like polypore famous for its glossy, varnished reddish-brown cap and prized in East Asian traditional medicine. It is too tough and woody to eat as food but is used as a medicinal decoction, tea, or extract. The name 'G. lucidum' has long been applied broadly, but molecular work shows it is a species complex; G. lucidum sensu stricto is European/temperate, while much non-Asian and cultivated material represents distinct species (e.g. G. lingzhi/G. sichuanense for the cultivated Asian taxon, G. curtisii and G. sessile in North America).
edibilityNotes: Not edible as a food: the fruiting body is woody, corky, and indigestible. It is non-poisonous and is used medicinally as a decoction (tea), tincture, or powdered extract rather than eaten whole. Not a culinary mushroom; medicinal claims are not evaluated here.
habitat: at the base of hardwood trees and stumps
distribution: Cosmopolitan as traditionally circumscribed, though true G. lucidum sensu stricto is European/temperate; many regional records represent distinct species within the G. lucidum complex.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ganoderma tsugae
dangerousLookalikes.note: Hemlock varnish shelf; nearly identical glossy varnished red-brown crust. Distinguished primarily by host (grows on conifers, especially hemlock/Tsuga) versus G. lucidum on hardwoods, and reliably only by genetics. Not toxic, but the most easily confused look-alike.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ganoderma curtisii
dangerousLookalikes.note: North American varnished polypore long misidentified as G. lucidum; distinguished by genetics and often a more elongated stipe and paler tones. Not dangerous, but a taxonomic look-alike.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ganoderma sichuanense
dangerousLookalikes.note: Linked to the cultivated Asian 'Lingzhi' (often treated as G. lingzhi); molecularly distinct from European G. lucidum. Visually very similar.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ganoderma applanatum
dangerousLookalikes.note: Artist's conk; lacks the glossy varnished crust and is perennial with a flat dull grey-brown upper surface and a white pore surface that bruises brown.

edibilityNotes: Choice edible, widely foraged. Must be thoroughly cooked; raw or undercooked specimens can cause gastrointestinal upset. Harvest only young, fresh, tender fruitbodies, as older specimens become tough and may host insects. As with all wild mushrooms, some people experience idiosyncratic GI reactions, so try a small portion first. Positive identification is required before eating any wild mushroom.
description: Grifola frondosa, known as maitake or hen of the woods, is a polypore that forms a large rosette of overlapping gray-brown spoon-shaped caps arising from a branched white stalk base. It is a prized choice edible studied for its beta-glucans, and it fruits at the base of hardwoods, especially oaks.
distribution: Widely distributed in the temperate deciduous forests of the Northern Hemisphere, including eastern North America, Europe, and East Asia (notably Japan and China).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Meripilus sumstinei (black-staining polypore)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Similar large rosette of overlapping caps at hardwood bases, but its flesh bruises and stains blackish when handled or cut, and caps are typically larger and more fan-shaped. Edible only when young and generally regarded as inferior and tougher; the black-staining reaction is the key separator from maitake.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Bondarzewia berkeleyi (Berkeley's polypore)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Forms large overlapping cream to tan caps at oak bases, but caps are much thicker, larger, and tougher with a corky texture; pores are much larger (visible to the naked eye) and it does not form the same dense thin-fronded rosette.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Laetiporus sulphureus (chicken of the woods)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Also a hardwood polypore, but bright orange and yellow rather than gray-brown, with broad shelving overlapping brackets rather than a gray rosette of small spoon-shaped caps.

Gyromitra esculenta, the false morel, is an ascomycete with a reddish-brown, brain-like wrinkled cap atop a pale stalk. Despite the epithet "esculenta" (meaning edible) and its traditional consumption in parts of Scandinavia and Eastern Europe after special processing, it contains gyromitrin and can be deadly.
edibilityNotes: Contains gyromitrin, which is hydrolyzed in the body to monomethylhydrazine (MMH), a hepatotoxic, neurotoxic, and carcinogenic compound. Onset of symptoms is DELAYED, typically 6-12 hours after ingestion: vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and vertigo, progressing in severe cases to liver failure, seizures, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, coma, and death. Toxin content is variable and there is no reliable safe dose. The toxin is volatile and only partly removed by parboiling and drying; poisoning has occurred even after such processing and from inhaling cooking vapors. Treated here as DEADLY and not recommended for consumption under any preparation.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including North America and Eurasia, especially in coniferous forests.

dangerousLookalikes.name: True morels (Morchella spp.)
dangerousLookalikes.note: The critical confusion: edible true morels have a honeycomb/pitted cap that is HOLLOW inside and continuous with a single hollow stem. Gyromitra esculenta has a solid, irregularly wrinkled/brain-like cap with chambered or stuffed (cotton-like) internal flesh, never a clean hollow cavity. Cut any "morel" lengthwise before eating; a non-hollow, cotton-stuffed interior indicates a dangerous false morel.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Gyromitra and false morels (e.g. Gyromitra gigas / Gyromitra montana group)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Other brain-like or saddle-shaped Gyromitra and related Discina/Helvella species are easily confused with G. esculenta and several also contain gyromitrin or have uncertain toxicity. Do not rely on species-level distinction in the field; treat all brain-shaped false morels as potentially toxic.

edibilityNotes: Edible and good when young, fresh, and white; cook before eating (do not eat raw). Mild, seafood-like flavor with a tender texture. Older specimens that have yellowed or browned become tough, bitter, or sour and are not worth collecting. As with any wild mushroom, eat only a small amount the first time. The whole genus Hericium is regarded as edible, so the species it can be confused with (other Hericium) are not toxic; still confirm you have a Hericium before eating.
description: Hericium coralloides, the coral tooth fungus, is a white, repeatedly branched, coral-like tooth fungus whose branches bear rows of short, hanging spines that release the spores. Fresh fruitbodies are pure white, yellowing or browning with age. It grows on the dead and dying wood of hardwoods (beech, maple, oak, and other broadleaf trees) as a saprotroph and wound parasite, producing a white rot, and fruits mainly in late summer and autumn across temperate forests of the Northern Hemisphere. Closely related to lion's mane (H. erinaceus), it differs in its openly branched, spreading habit with spines along the branches rather than in a single dense clump. It is a choice edible when young and white. It has no dangerous (toxic) lookalikes; the similar species are other edible Hericium.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including North America, Europe, and Asia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hericium erinaceus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Lion's mane; also edible, not dangerous. Forms a single unbranched cushion with long spines hanging like a pom-pom rather than the coral-like branched habit of H. coralloides.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hericium americanum
dangerousLookalikes.note: Also edible, not dangerous. Very similar branched form but with fewer, thicker branches and longer spines; mainly an eastern North American species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hericium abietis
dangerousLookalikes.note: Also edible, not dangerous. Bear's-head Hericium; large branched fruitbody, but grows on conifer wood rather than hardwoods.

description: Hericium erinaceus is a toothed fungus that forms a single rounded, unbranched white cushion bearing long, cascading, icicle-like spines. It is prized as a choice edible with a seafood-like (crab or lobster) flavor and texture, and is studied for compounds (hericenones and erinacines) reported to stimulate nerve growth factor (NGF) synthesis in laboratory settings.
edibilityNotes: Choice edible, best cooked; flesh is sliced and sauteed, developing a seafood-like flavor. Cook thoroughly before eating. Harvest while white and firm; older yellowing or browning specimens turn sour and unpleasant. As with all wild fungi, confirm identity before consuming.
habitat: wounds and scars on living hardwoods
distribution: Widespread across temperate forests of the Northern Hemisphere, including North America, Europe, and East Asia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hericium coralloides
dangerousLookalikes.note: Coral tooth fungus: much-branched with spines clustered along the branches, rather than a single unbranched cushion of long hanging spines. Also edible, so not a safety hazard.

dangerousLookalikes.note: Bear's head tooth: branched with longer spines than H. coralloides. Also edible; distinguished by its branching habit versus the single unbranched mass of H. erinaceus.

edibilityNotes: A well-regarded edible recognized by the soft spines (teeth) on the cap underside rather than gills or pores, which separates it from all deadly gilled mushrooms (e.g. Amanita). Older or large specimens can be bitter; cook thoroughly, and parboil older fruitbodies if bitterness persists. It has no deadly lookalikes. The only toothed look-alikes to be aware of are other spine-bearing fungi: bitter/acrid Sarcodon species and woody Hydnellum species, which are unpalatable or inedible rather than poisonous. Always cook before eating and confirm the toothed hymenophore.
description: Hydnum repandum, the hedgehog or sweet tooth mushroom, is an edible ectomycorrhizal fungus recognized by the soft spines (teeth) lining the underside of its buff to pale-orange cap instead of gills or pores. The toothed hymenophore distinguishes it from deadly gilled mushrooms, making it a relatively safe choice for foragers who confirm the teeth.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe and North America.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Sarcodon spp. (e.g. Sarcodon scabrosus, S. squamosus)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Also toothed/spine-bearing, but typically larger with a scaly cap and a bitter or acrid taste; not deadly but unpalatable and can cause gastrointestinal upset. Distinguished by taste, scaly cap, and tougher flesh.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hydnellum spp.
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toothed fungi with tough, woody, often zonate flesh; inedible due to texture and bitterness rather than toxic. Distinguished by their corky/woody consistency.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hydnum rufescens
dangerousLookalikes.note: A closely related, edible toothed fungus that is smaller and more orange-brown; not dangerous, a benign edible relative often treated as a close ally.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hydnum umbilicatum
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another edible Hydnum with a smaller, often umbilicate (navel-depressed) cap and slender stipe; harmless and also edible.

description: Hydnum repandum subsp. rufescens is a species of fungus in the genus Hydnum, family Hydnaceae, order Cantharellales, class Agaricomycetes, phylum Basidiomycota.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hydnum repandum
dangerousLookalikes.note: Confusable with Hydnum repandum (edible). See its profile for how to tell them apart.

edibilityNotes: Toxic. Causes gastrointestinal illness (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea), sometimes with delayed onset, associated with fasciculol-type triterpene compounds. The flesh is also intensely and persistently bitter, which usually deters consumption. Not a food species under any preparation. Its habit of growing in dense clusters on wood alongside genuinely edible species (and the deadly Galerina marginata) makes misidentification a real risk.
description: Sulphur Tuft (Hypholoma fasciculare) is a common, widespread wood-rotting mushroom that fruits in dense, crowded clusters on dead hardwood and conifer stumps, logs, and buried roots. Caps are typically 2–6 cm across, convex to flattened, sulphur-yellow to greenish-yellow and often more orange-brown or tan toward the centre. The crowded gills start sulphur-yellow, become distinctly green to olive-tinged with age, and finally turn purple-brown as the spores mature. The slender yellowish stems are often rusty-stained below and frequently fused at the base in the cluster; a faint fibrillose ring zone may be present from the cortina-like partial veil. The spore print is purple-brown. The flesh is yellow and intensely bitter. It is a saprotroph, fruiting from spring through autumn (mainly late summer to late autumn) and sometimes in mild winters, and is one of the most frequently encountered cluster-forming wood mushrooms in temperate woodlands. It is toxic and not edible.
distribution: Cosmopolitan and very common across temperate regions, including Europe, North America, Asia, and Australasia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hypholoma capnoides
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible. Grows on conifer wood; gills are greyish to smoky-grey (never green-tinged) before turning purple-brown, and the flesh is mild rather than bitter.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hypholoma lateritium
dangerousLookalikes.note: Brick Cap. Reputedly edible (cook; some sources caution), clusters on hardwood; cap is brick-red to tan with a paler margin and the flesh is mild rather than the intensely bitter taste of Sulphur Tuft.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY (amatoxins). Also clusters on dead wood but has a rusty-brown spore print (not purple-brown), a browner cap, and a more distinct membranous ring. Lethal if eaten.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Armillaria mellea
dangerousLookalikes.note: Honey fungus. Clusters on wood/roots but is honey-brown with a whitish spore print, a persistent ring, and fine dark scales on the cap; edible only when thoroughly cooked.

Imleria badia, the Bay Bolete, is a pored mushroom of conifer and mixed woodland, long known under the name Boletus badius before being moved to the genus Imleria. It has a chestnut to bay-brown cap that is finely velvety or suede-like when dry and somewhat sticky when wet, growing roughly 4-15 cm across. The underside bears pores (tubes), not gills, which are cream to pale yellow and bruise blue-green to dull bluish on touch or with age. The stipe is paler brown, fibrous and often streaky, without a ring and without a coarse net. It is a popular, good edible when thoroughly cooked, with a mild nutty flavour, but should never be eaten raw. The main confusion species to rule out is the bitter Tylopilus felleus, which has pinkish pores and an intensely bitter taste; always confirm pores rather than gills and check for the characteristic blue-green bruising.
edibilityNotes: A well-regarded edible bolete that must be cooked before eating; raw boletes can cause gastrointestinal upset. The bluing reaction of the pores is normal for this species and not a sign of toxicity. As with all foraged fungi, eat only after a confident identification and try a small portion first. Like many wild mushrooms it can accumulate heavy metals and radiocaesium, so avoid harvesting from contaminated or roadside sites and eat in moderation.
distribution: Widespread across Europe and present in North America; reported more broadly across temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Tylopilus felleus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Bitter bolete; pores are whitish then pinkish (not yellow and not bruising blue-green), stipe bears a coarse dark net, and the flesh is intensely bitter, making it inedible. A bitter taste test on a tiny piece readily separates it. Not deadly but will ruin a dish.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Boletus / Imleria species with red pores
dangerousLookalikes.note: Bay Bolete always has cream-to-yellow pores. Any bolete with orange-to-red pore mouths (e.g. Suillellus / Rubroboletus group) should be left alone unless separately confirmed, as several red-pored, blue-staining boletes are toxic raw or outright poisonous.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Hortiboletus / Xerocomellus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several smaller brown, blue-bruising boletes in the Xerocomus group resemble young Bay Bolete. They are not dangerous but are easily confused; the Bay Bolete is distinguished by its larger size, tacky cap when wet, and prompt blue-green bruising of cream-yellow pores.
