edibilityNotes: Not a culinary mushroom. The sterile conk is woody/corky and is never eaten as food; it is used only as a brewed extract, decoction, or tea in folk and supplement contexts. Medicinal and safety claims are not established by rigorous clinical evidence; high oxalate content has been linked to kidney injury (oxalate nephropathy) with heavy or prolonged use, and it may interact with anticoagulants and affect blood sugar. Harvest only from living birch and observe sustainability concerns.
description: Inonotus obliquus, commonly called Chaga, is a wood-decay fungus best known not as a fruiting mushroom but as a sterile conk (sclerotium): a hard, blackened, deeply cracked charcoal-like mass that erupts from the trunk of living birch trees. The exterior is brittle and coal-black from accumulated melanin, while the interior is a rusty orange-brown, corky tissue. This conk is sterile vegetative tissue, not the spore-producing body; the true fruiting body (a resupinate, pored hymenium) forms inconspicuously beneath the bark, usually after the host tree dies, and is rarely seen. The fungus is a slow parasite, taking many years to develop a harvestable conk and ultimately contributing to the host tree's decline (a white rot). It has a long history in folk medicine across northern Eurasia, where the ground conk is brewed as a dark, slightly bitter tea or decoction valued for its antioxidant content. Reported constituents include melanin, polysaccharides (beta-glucans), polyphenols, and triterpenes such as betulin and betulinic acid that the fungus concentrates from the birch host, along with inotodiol. It is woody and inedible as food; its use is strictly as a brewed extract, and purported health benefits are not confirmed by robust clinical trials. Because demand has driven heavy wild collection and the conk regenerates very slowly, sustainable and ethical harvesting from living birch is a real conservation concern.
substrate: Standing birch wood; rarely other hardwoods
hosts: occasionally Alnus, Fagus, Ulmus and other hardwoods (less valued)
habitat: Boreal and northern temperate birch forests
distribution: Circumboreal: widespread across the cooler regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including northern and eastern Europe, Russia and Siberia, northern Asia, and northern North America (Canada and the northern United States), wherever birch grows.
sporePrintColor: pale yellowish to brownish (from the rarely observed fertile crust)

dangerousLookalikes.name: Burl / tree gall on birch
dangerousLookalikes.note: Woody outgrowths and burls can superficially resemble a Chaga conk but are smooth and bark-covered, lacking the black cracked crust and the rusty-orange brittle interior. Mistaking inert wood for Chaga wastes harvest effort but is not toxic.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Phellinus / Fomes bracket fungi
dangerousLookalikes.note: Hard perennial brackets (e.g. Phellinus igniarius, Fomes fomentarius) grow on birch and other hardwoods but form a distinct hoof- or shelf-shaped fruiting body with a pored underside, not the irregular black sterile sclerotium of Chaga. They lack the rusty-orange interior and are not used as Chaga.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Inonotus / Phaeolus rusty-fleshed polypores
dangerousLookalikes.note: Other Inonotus species and rusty-brown polypores can share the orange-brown flesh tone but form true fleshy/poroid brackets rather than a hard black cracked external conk on living birch.

edibilityNotes: Edible and well regarded, especially in Spain/Catalonia (the prized "rovelló"), Provence, and across the Mediterranean and Eastern Europe. Always cook it; raw or undercooked Lactarius can cause gastrointestinal upset, and texture improves with grilling, frying, or roasting. The flesh and orange latex stain greenish on handling/aging, which is normal and not a sign of toxicity. The pigments may also harmlessly turn urine orange-red after a meal. Some find it slightly bitter or grainy. Always confirm identification before eating, as several related milkcaps are acrid and unpalatable; the key safe-group traits are carrot-orange latex (not white), a mild (non-acrid) taste, and pine association.
description: Lactarius deliciosus, the Saffron Milk Cap, is a brightly colored ectomycorrhizal mushroom associated with pines. The cap is carrot- to saffron-orange, often with darker concentric zones (zonate), 4-12 cm or more across, becoming funnel-shaped or depressed with age and frequently developing greenish blotches where bruised or aging. The gills and stem are also orange, and the hollow stem may show shallow orange pits (scrobicules). Its defining feature is the latex ("milk"): when the flesh or gills are cut, it exudes a bright carrot-orange latex that slowly stains the tissue greenish on exposure to air. It is one of the few choice edible members of the genus Lactarius, most of which are acrid or peppery. Fruiting bodies appear from late summer through autumn in coniferous woodland, particularly under pines on calcareous or sandy soils. Note: North American records named L. deliciosus largely represent closely related, distinct species rather than the European type.
distribution: Native to Europe; widespread across the continent, especially the Mediterranean. Introduced and naturalized elsewhere (e.g. with planted pines in parts of Australia, New Zealand, and South America). The name "Lactarius deliciosus" has historically been applied broadly to similar orange-milk milkcaps worldwide; many non-European records (notably in North America) represent closely related but distinct species in the same group.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Lactarius semisanguifluus

dangerousLookalikes.name: Lactarius torminosus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Woolly milkcap: pinkish cap with a shaggy inrolled margin, WHITE acrid latex (not orange), typically under birch. Causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea/vomiting) if eaten raw or undercooked. The clearest separator from the saffron milkcap is white vs orange latex.

edibilityNotes: Edible and consumed in parts of Mexico, Guatemala, China, and the United States, where it is sold in rural markets. Should be cooked before eating; the firm flesh is best sliced thin, and the blue color fades with cooking. Flavor is described as mild but somewhat slightly peppery or bitter, and texture as coarse or grainy; quality is rated anywhere from superior to mediocre. As with all wild mushrooms, positively confirm identity before consuming.
description: Lactarius indigo, the indigo milk cap, is a strikingly distinctive ectomycorrhizal mushroom that is entirely indigo to dark blue when fresh, becoming paler and greenish with age and handling. The cap is 5-15 cm wide, convex to vase-shaped (depressed at the center) at maturity, often with concentric darker zones, and a sticky surface when moist. The closely spaced gills are indigo blue and run down the stem (decurrent). When cut or broken, the flesh exudes a milky latex that is itself a remarkable dark indigo blue, which slowly stains the wounded tissue green upon exposure to air. The stem is blue, often hollow at maturity, and the whole mushroom commonly bruises and discolors green over time. The blue color, blue latex, and green staining make it one of the most readily recognizable mushrooms, with few dangerous lookalikes. The blue pigment is attributed to the azulene derivative (7-isopropenyl-4-methylazulen-1-yl)methyl stearate.
habitat: forms ectomycorrhizal associations with trees, especially oak and pine
distribution: Southern and eastern North America, Mexico, Central America (Guatemala, Costa Rica) and into South America (Colombia), and Asia (China, India). Reported from southern France in Europe.

edibilityNotes: Edible and considered choice ONLY when young, tender, and thoroughly cooked; the meaty texture earns the name "chicken of the woods." A significant minority of people experience adverse reactions even from well-cooked hardwood specimens: gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, cramps), dizziness, and swelling of the lips/face. Reactions appear idiosyncratic, so always cook thoroughly and eat only a small amount the first time, then wait before eating more. AVOID specimens growing on conifers, yew (Taxus, which is itself highly toxic), eucalyptus, or black locust (Robinia) — these are more strongly associated with poisonings, and conifer-growing chicken-of-the-woods are now recognized as separate species (e.g. Laetiporus conifericola/huroniensis) that should not be eaten. Do not eat older, tough, or insect-infested brackets.
description: Laetiporus sulphureus, known as chicken of the woods or sulphur shelf, is a bright orange-and-yellow bracket fungus that fruits in overlapping tiers on hardwoods, especially oak. It has no gills; the underside is a sulphur-yellow pore surface. Young, well-cooked specimens are prized as an edible with a chicken-like texture, though a notable minority of people react badly to it.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, notably Europe and eastern North America. In North America the broader complex has been split into several segregate species, and true L. sulphureus is best applied to hardwood-growing, yellow-pored material.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus illudens (eastern jack-o'-lantern)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Bright orange and grows on/near hardwood, but it is a GILLED mushroom (true decurrent gills, not pores), forms clustered stemmed caps rather than shelving brackets, and is toxic (causes severe GI illness). Always confirm a yellow PORE surface and shelf form, not gills.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Conifer-growing Laetiporus (e.g. L. conifericola, L. huroniensis)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Look nearly identical to chicken of the woods but grow on conifers. These are now treated as distinct species and are more frequently linked to poisonings; do not eat brackets fruiting on conifers, yew, or eucalyptus.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Laetiporus cincinnatus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous — an edible relative. Forms rosettes at the base of oaks with a white to pale cream (not sulphur-yellow) pore surface. Listed to distinguish it, not as a hazard.

Leccinum scabrum (Brown Birch Bolete) is a birch-associated ectomycorrhizal bolete with a tan to grey-brown cap, whitish pores, and a pale stem covered in dark scabers. The soft flesh may darken on cutting and turns blackish on cooking. Edible only when thoroughly cooked; of modest culinary quality.
edibilityNotes: Edible ONLY when thoroughly cooked. Raw or undercooked boletes of this group can cause gastrointestinal upset, so always cook well before eating. The flesh is soft and mild; older specimens become spongy and waterlogged and are best discarded or used only for drying. Within the scaber-stalk (Leccinum) complex, several segregate species are difficult to separate; L. scabrum itself is regarded as a safe edible but is unremarkable in flavour. As with any wild fungus, identify with certainty and eat only a small portion when trying a species for the first time.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, the Himalayas, northern Asia, and North America, wherever birch occurs; also introduced with planted birch in parts of the Southern Hemisphere (notably Australia and New Zealand).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Leccinum scaber-stalks (e.g. Leccinum variicolor, Leccinum holopus, Leccinum oxydabile)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Closely related birch-associated scaber stalks, also edible-when-cooked, separated by cap colour, flesh staining (e.g. blue-green stipe base in L. variicolor) and habitat. Not dangerous, but the group is a complex rather than a single clean species; all require thorough cooking.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Tylopilus felleus (Bitter Bolete)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Superficially bolete-like with a brown cap, but has a coarse dark net (reticulation) on the stem rather than discrete scabers, pores that flush pinkish with age, and an intensely bitter taste that ruins a dish. Not deadly but renders food inedible.

Shiitake is a choice edible wood-decay mushroom native to East Asia and one of the most widely cultivated mushrooms in the world, grown on hardwood logs and supplemented sawdust. It has a brown, often scaly cap, whitish gills, and a fibrous stem, and is valued both as food and for medicinal interest in its polysaccharide lentinan.
edibilityNotes: Choice edible only when thoroughly cooked. Eating raw or undercooked shiitake can cause shiitake (flagellate) dermatitis — a self-limiting but intensely itchy whip-lash/linear streak rash, typically appearing within 1-5 days of ingestion. It is attributed to lentinan, a heat-labile polysaccharide; thorough cooking degrades it and prevents the reaction. A minority of people may also experience digestive upset. Always cook shiitake fully before eating.
distribution: Native to warm, moist regions of East Asia (Japan, China, Korea) and Southeast Asia; now cultivated and consumed worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus species (jack-o'-lantern)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic jack-o'-lanterns are bright orange throughout with crowded, decurrent gills, grow in dense clusters on wood, and lack shiitake's brown scaly cap and white-ish adnexed gills. Wild brown-capped, gilled mushrooms on hardwood should be identified carefully before eating.

The Wood Blewit (Lepista nuda, also placed in Clitocybe/Collybia and historically in Tricholoma) is a medium-to-large agaric recognizable by its lilac to violet-blue coloration when young. The cap is smooth, domed becoming flattened, about 5-15 cm across, lilac-tinged fading to tan or buff-brown with age and drying. The crowded, sinuate gills and the fibrous, often bulbous-based stem share the violet hue when fresh. The flesh is thick with a distinctive sweetish, fruity-perfumed odour often likened to frozen orange juice. It is a late-season mushroom, fruiting from autumn into winter and tolerant of light frost, typically in troops or arcs/rings in leaf litter, compost, and humus-rich ground in both deciduous and coniferous woodland as well as gardens and hedgerows. Crucially for identification, the spore print is pale pinkish to pinkish-buff. A popular edible that must be cooked thoroughly, it has toxic lilac/purple lookalikes among the Cortinarius webcaps (separated chiefly by rusty-brown spore print and a cortina) and can be confused, when old or faded, with small white muscarine-containing Clitocybe.
edibilityNotes: Edible and well regarded, but ONLY after thorough cooking (at least about 15-20 minutes). Raw or undercooked specimens contain heat-labile compounds that cause gastrointestinal upset; never eat raw. A minority of people experience indigestion or allergic reaction even when it is properly cooked, so eat only a small amount the first time and avoid alcohol with an unfamiliar batch. Always confirm the pale pinkish to pinkish-buff spore print, the lack of a cortina, and the lack of a white spore print before eating: rusty-brown spores with a cobwebby cortina indicate a Cortinarius webcap (some contain the deadly nephrotoxin orellanine), and a white spore print on a small pale specimen may indicate a muscarine-containing Clitocybe.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe and North America; also introduced and naturalized in parts of Australia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Cortinarius webcaps (purple/lilac species)
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY potential. Several purple/violet Cortinarius species resemble young blewits but have a RUSTY-BROWN spore print (vs. pale pink in Lepista nuda) and a cortina (cobweb-like partial veil) that leaves rusty fibres on the stem. Members of the orellanine-containing group (e.g. the C. rubellus / C. orellanus complex) cause delayed, often fatal kidney failure with onset days after ingestion. Spore print colour plus the cortina are the decisive separators.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Violet webcap (Cortinarius violaceus)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Deep violet throughout with a dry, scaly cap, a cortina, and a rusty-brown spore print. Not in the deadly orellanine group but not recommended for eating; the rusty spores and cortina distinguish it from the pink-spored, cortina-free blewit.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ivory/fool's funnel (Clitocybe rivulosa / C. dealbata)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small white-to-buff funnel mushrooms that can be confused with old or faded blewits, especially in grass and on lawns. They contain dangerous amounts of muscarine (sweating, salivation, tearing within ~15-30 min; deaths recorded) and give a WHITE spore print rather than pinkish-buff. Size, lack of lilac tones, and white spores separate them.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Lilac fibrecap (Inocybe geophylla var. lilacina)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A small lilac mushroom, much smaller than a blewit, with a conical/umbonate cap, dull clay-brown spore print, and toxic muscarine. Size and brown spores separate it.

Lycoperdon perlatum, the common puffball or gem-studded puffball, is a widespread saprotrophic fungus in the family Agaricaceae. The fruiting body is whitish to pale grey-brown, pear-shaped to top-shaped, typically 1.5-6 cm wide and 3-7 cm tall, with a rounded head tapering to a sterile stem-like base. The outer surface is covered in detachable conical spines (warts) interspersed with smaller granular warts; when the spines fall away they leave a net-like pattern of pale scars. At maturity a pore opens at the apex through which the spores are released, often in puffs when struck by raindrops or pressure. The interior (gleba) is pure white and firm-fleshy when young, turning yellowish, then olive-brown and powdery as the spores mature. It is edible only in the young stage while the gleba is uniformly white; it must be cooked and should never be eaten once any yellowing or browning has begun.
edibilityNotes: Edible ONLY when young and the interior is pure white, firm, and completely homogeneous; it must be cooked before eating. Once the gleba shows any yellow, olive, or brown discoloration it is past edibility and should be discarded (spore maturation has begun). CRITICAL CUT-TEST: before eating any small white puffball-like fungus, slice it vertically from top to bottom. A true puffball shows a uniform, soft, pure-white interior with no internal structure. (1) If the cut reveals the silhouette of a developing cap, gills, and stem, it is the immature "button"/"egg" stage of an Amanita (potentially the deadly Amanita phalloides or A. virosa) and must NOT be eaten. (2) If the interior is firm and dark (purplish-black to greyish), often marbled, it is a Scleroderma earthball, which is toxic. Discard any specimen that is not uniformly soft and pure white inside. Note: unlike many gilled edibles, puffballs carry no coprine/alcohol-reaction or muscarine concerns — the sole serious hazards are the Amanita-egg and earthball confusions identified by the cut test.
distribution: Cosmopolitan and very common; nearly worldwide, including North America (Alaska to Mexico), Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and South America. Most abundant in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides (death cap) button/egg stage
dangerousLookalikes.note: An immature Amanita egg can superficially resemble a small white puffball. A vertical cut reveals the outline of a developing cap, gills, and stem inside; a true puffball is uniformly white and structureless throughout. Amanita phalloides is deadly poisonous (amatoxins). Always cut-test.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita virosa (destroying angel) button/egg stage
dangerousLookalikes.note: Like the death cap, the immature egg can be mistaken for a puffball. A vertical cut shows an internal capped, gilled silhouette. Deadly poisonous (amatoxins).

dangerousLookalikes.name: Scleroderma citrinum (common earthball)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Earthballs are firmer with a thick tough rind and a dark purplish-black to grey, often marbled, interior that develops much earlier than a puffball's, lacking the soft white homogeneous gleba and conical spines of a young Lycoperdon. They break apart rather than releasing spores through an apical pore. Toxic, causing gastrointestinal poisoning.

Macrolepiota procera, the Parasol Mushroom, is a large, choice edible mushroom with a tall stem bearing a distinctive snakeskin (brownish, banded) pattern and a movable double ring. It has a broad, scaly cap, white spore print, free gills, and no volva, and typically grows solitary or in groups in grassy clearings, pastures, and forest edges.
distribution: Widespread in temperate regions of Europe, North America, and Asia, and reported from other temperate areas worldwide.
edibilityNotes: A choice edible, but eat only the caps thoroughly cooked and discard the tough, fibrous stem; never eat raw. CRITICAL: confirm a white spore print and the complete absence of a volva before eating. The green-spored parasol (Chlorophyllum molybdites) is a common cause of serious gastrointestinal poisoning and has a GREEN spore print. More dangerously, young, unexpanded parasols can be confused with DEADLY Amanita species (e.g., the death cap and destroying angels), which have a VOLVA (cup or bulb at the stem base), often a smooth (non-snakeskin) stem, and may give a white spore print. Always check the stem base for a volva and take a spore print.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chlorophyllum molybdites
dangerousLookalikes.note: Green-spored parasol; one of the most common causes of mushroom poisoning in North America (severe GI distress, not deadly). Distinguished by a GREEN spore print (vs. white in M. procera) and gills that age greenish; lacks the strongly snakeskin-banded stem. Always take a spore print.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita species (young/button stage)
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY Amanitas (death cap A. phalloides, destroying angels A. bisporigera/virosa) can resemble young unexpanded parasols. Amanitas have a VOLVA (membranous cup or bulb at the stem base) and a smooth (not snakeskin-patterned) stem. Always dig up the full stem base and check for a volva.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chlorophyllum brunneum
dangerousLookalikes.note: Shaggy parasol relative with an abrupt-bulbous stem base and a typically single (not movable double) ring; can cause gastrointestinal upset in some people.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Chlorophyllum rhacodes
dangerousLookalikes.note: Shaggy parasol; flesh reddens/bruises when cut and the stem lacks the snakeskin banding of M. procera. Generally edible when cooked but causes GI upset in some individuals; confirm white spore print.

Marasmius oreades, the Fairy Ring Champignon (also called Scotch Bonnet or Mousseron), is a small, tough-fleshed agaric that grows gregariously in rings and arcs across lawns, pastures, and other short grassland. The cap is 1-5 cm across, bell-shaped to broadly convex with a low central umbo, smooth, and tan to buff or pale cream — hygrophanous, darkening and appearing more brownish when moist and drying paler. A hallmark is its marasmioid resilience: fruitbodies shrivel in drought and revive to release spores when rehydrated. The gills are notably broad, pale whitish to cream, and widely spaced (distant), and are free to nearly free from the stem. The stem is slender, tough, pliable and wiry, whitish to pale buff, and does not snap cleanly. The spore print is white to whitish/cream. It has a pleasant odor, sometimes described as sweet or with a hint of hydrogen cyanide (HCN / bitter-almond) when cut or crushed. A classic edible prized for soups and sauces, but typically only the caps are used because the wiry stems are too tough and fibrous; cook before eating. The overriding caution is identification: M. oreades shares lawns and grassland with several small whitish mushrooms that are dangerously toxic — especially muscarine-containing Clitocybe (e.g., C. rivulosa / C. dealbata), which have crowded, decurrent white gills (versus the distant, free, broad gills of M. oreades). Beginners must learn these distinctions before eating.
edibilityNotes: Edible and well regarded, but cook before eating and use mainly the caps — the wiry stems are too tough. The serious risk is misidentification: M. oreades fruits in the same lawns and grassland as toxic look-alikes. Most important is the muscarine-containing "lawn/sweating" Clitocybe group (Clitocybe rivulosa / C. dealbata), which causes rapid-onset muscarinic (SLUDGE-type, profuse sweating/salivation) poisoning. Key separating features of M. oreades: broad, widely spaced (distant) pale gills that are free to nearly free; a tough, pliable stem that does not snap; a hygrophanous tan cap with a low umbo; and the ability to revive after drying. Toxic lawn Clitocybe instead have crowded, decurrent white gills and a flatter, often chalky-white cap. Other small whitish grassland fungi (including some deadly amatoxin-containing Lepiota/dapperlings and muscarine-containing white Inocybe fibrecaps) can also occur nearby. Never eat any small white/tan lawn mushroom unless every feature matches M. oreades and the muscarine and amatoxin look-alikes are confidently excluded.
distribution: Widespread and common across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe and North America; reported widely in grassy habitats in many temperate regions worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Clitocybe rivulosa
dangerousLookalikes.note: Toxic lawn species containing muscarine. Grows in the same grass, often in rings. Distinguished by crowded, decurrent white gills (vs. M. oreades' broad, distant, free gills) and a flatter, chalky whitish, sometimes faintly zoned cap. Causes muscarinic (SLUDGE/profuse sweating) poisoning.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Clitocybe dealbata
dangerousLookalikes.note: Closely allied muscarine-containing lawn Clitocybe, often treated together with C. rivulosa (and sometimes considered synonymous). Crowded decurrent gills and a white cap; toxic. A primary cause of confusion for fairy-ring foragers.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Lepiota species (small white dapperlings)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some small grassland Lepiota (e.g. members of the L. brunneoincarnata / L. helveola group) contain deadly amatoxins. Differ from M. oreades in having a stem ring and finely scaly caps; can occur in grassy/disturbed ground.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Inocybe species (white fibrecaps)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several small whitish Inocybe contain muscarine and occur in grass and at grassy woodland edges. Differ by radially fibrous/silky caps, an earthy or spermatic smell, and a dull brown (not white) spore print.

The yellow morel is a prized edible ascomycete with a distinctive pale tan to yellowish-brown honeycomb cap whose pits and ridges form a network of irregular chambers. The hollow cap is fully attached to the hollow stipe, and the whole fruitbody is hollow when sliced lengthwise. It must be thoroughly cooked before eating, as raw specimens cause gastrointestinal upset.
edibilityNotes: Choice edible ONLY when thoroughly cooked. Raw or undercooked morels contain heat-labile, hemolytic toxins that cause nausea, vomiting, and other gastrointestinal distress. Reactions have also been reported when morels are consumed with alcohol. Always cook fully, eat a small amount the first time, and never consume raw. Before eating, cut the fruitbody lengthwise and confirm it is completely hollow from cap to stem base with the cap fully fused to the stem, to rule out the toxic false morels (Gyromitra) and Verpa species.
habitat: near ash, elm, apple, and poplar trees
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including much of North America and Europe.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Gyromitra esculenta (false morel)
dangerousLookalikes.note: False morels have a brain-like or saddle-shaped, irregularly wrinkled and lobed reddish-brown cap (not a regular pitted honeycomb), and the interior is chambered/stuffed with wispy cottony tissue rather than a single clean hollow chamber. They contain gyromitrin (metabolized to monomethylhydrazine) and can be deadly. When in doubt, cut the fruitbody lengthwise: true morels are completely hollow.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Verpa species (early/false morel, e.g. Verpa bohemica, Verpa conica)
dangerousLookalikes.note: In Verpa the cap hangs free, attached to the stem only at the very top like a thimble or skirt, whereas in true morels the lower edge of the cap is fully fused to the stem. Verpa can cause gastrointestinal upset and loss of muscle coordination in some people.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Morchella elata / black morel group
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible true morels but worth distinguishing for ID; black morels have darker ridges and longer, vertically aligned pits. Cook thoroughly as with all morels.

Panaeolus cyanescens, commonly called Blue Meanie, is a potent psilocybin- and psilocin-containing mushroom of tropical and subtropical pastures. It is coprophilous, fruiting on dung, with a pale grey to brownish cap that often cracks when dry, strong blue-green bruising, and a black spore print. It is psychoactive and controlled in many jurisdictions; its main danger is confusion with small brown dung/grassland mushrooms, some of which are deadly.
distribution: Pantropical and subtropical distribution; found in suitable warm, humid regions worldwide including the southern United States, Central and South America, the Caribbean, parts of Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia.
edibilityNotes: Psychoactive — contains psilocybin and psilocin, often at high potency. Not consumed as food. Psilocybin and psilocin are controlled substances in many countries, making possession and cultivation illegal in numerous jurisdictions. Effects include marked alterations in perception, mood, and cognition; risks include nausea, anxiety, and dangerous misidentification. The greatest hazard is confusion with small brown dung- or grassland-dwelling mushrooms ("LBMs"), some of which are deadly poisonous (e.g. amatoxin-containing Conocybe and Galerina). Strong blue-green bruising and a black spore print are key but not foolproof field characters; never consume any wild mushroom without expert verification.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Conocybe filaris
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small grassland/lawn mushroom containing deadly amatoxins (the same toxins as the death cap). Has a rusty- to cinnamon-brown spore print, a movable ring on the stem, and does not bruise blue. Amatoxin poisoning causes delayed (6–24 h) onset, deceptive recovery, then potentially fatal liver and kidney failure.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small brown mushrooms; several (e.g. Galerina marginata) contain deadly amatoxins. Typically grow on wood/moss rather than dung, have a rusty-brown spore print (not black), a ring, and do not bruise blue. Amatoxin toxicity is delayed and can be fatal.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Panaeolus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several Panaeolus species share the dung habitat, dark spore print, and small grey-brown caps. Some contain psilocybin and some do not; potency and legality vary. Strong blue bruising is more pronounced in P. cyanescens.

edibilityNotes: DEADLY. Paxillus involutus causes Paxillus syndrome, a cumulative, immune-mediated (autoimmune) hemolytic anemia. Sensitization builds over repeated meals, so the reaction can appear unpredictably after months or years of eating it without any prior symptoms. Cooking does NOT make it safe. Once an episode is triggered, gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain) typically begin within 1-3 hours and can progress to massive intravascular hemolysis, acute kidney failure, shock, and death. It was historically eaten in parts of Europe after parboiling; that practice is now considered dangerous and the mushroom should never be consumed.
description: The Brown Roll-rim, a medium to large brown gilled mushroom with a strongly inrolled, felty cap margin and decurrent gills that bruise dark brown when handled. Once treated as edible after cooking, it is now recognized as deadly because of Paxillus syndrome, a cumulative immune-mediated hemolytic reaction that can strike after years of uneventful consumption.
distribution: Widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere (Europe, Asia, and North America), and introduced elsewhere with planted trees, including Australia and South America.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Paxillus rubicundulus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another roll-rim with similar form and also considered unsafe; associated with alder (Alnus) and has a more scaly/squamulose cap.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Tapinella atrotomentosa (Velvet Roll-rim)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Grows on conifer wood/stumps and has a thick dark velvety stipe; distinguished by its lignicolous habit and dark felty stalk. Not recommended for eating.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Lactarius species (milkcaps)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some brown Lactarius have decurrent gills and similar coloration but exude milky latex when the gills are cut, which Paxillus never does.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Suillus luteus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Confusable with Suillus luteus (edible). See its profile for how to tell them apart.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Phallus impudicus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Confusable with Phallus impudicus (edible). See its profile for how to tell them apart.

description: Phallus hadriani is a species of fungus in the genus Phallus, family Phallaceae, order Phallales, class Agaricomycetes, phylum Basidiomycota.

Phallus impudicus, the Common Stinkhorn, is a widespread saprotrophic fungus famous for its rapid, phallic fruiting body and the powerful, fetid odor it emits at maturity. The fungus first appears as a partly buried whitish to off-white "egg" 4-6 cm across, attached to the soil by a white mycelial cord (rhizomorph). From this egg the fruiting body erupts rapidly, the spongy white stalk (receptacle) elongating to 10-25 cm in a matter of hours. The stalk is capped with a thimble-like, ridged/honeycombed cap coated in a slimy, olive-green to brown spore mass called the gleba. The gleba smells strongly of carrion/rotting flesh, attracting flies and other insects that feed on it and disperse the spores; once the slime is removed by insects the underlying white cap is exposed. It is a common species of woodlands, gardens, hedgerows, mulched beds, and wood-debris-rich soils across Europe, North America, and beyond, fruiting mainly in summer and autumn.

EDIBILITY AND SAFETY: Only the immature "egg" stage is eaten, and only as a regional novelty. When sliced, the egg reveals a firm white outer skin, a thick gelatinous (jelly-like) layer, and a darker olive-green embryonic gleba/stalk in the center. The crisp inner core is sometimes eaten raw (reportedly radish-like) or cooked; the gelatinous layer is typically peeled away. The mature stinkhorn, with its slimy gleba, is not eaten. CRITICAL CUT TEST: an unopened stinkhorn egg can superficially resemble the egg/button (volva-enclosed young fruiting body) of a deadly Amanita such as the Death Cap (Amanita phalloides) or Destroying Angel (Amanita virosa). ALWAYS slice any white "egg" vertically from top to bottom before considering it: a stinkhorn egg shows a gelatinous layer surrounding an undifferentiated olive embryonic structure, whereas an Amanita button shows a clearly differentiated, developing gilled mushroom (cap, gills, stem) in cross-section. If a young gilled mushroom is visible inside, discard it — it is not a stinkhorn. When in doubt, do not eat.
edibilityNotes: Edible only at the immature white "egg" stage, and only as a regional novelty; the crisp inner core is eaten raw (radish-like flavor) or cooked, with the gelatinous outer layer peeled away. The mature stalk with its foul-smelling olive gleba is not consumed. SAFETY-CRITICAL: an unopened white stinkhorn egg can resemble the button of a deadly Amanita (Death Cap, Destroying Angel). Always slice the egg vertically before eating — a stinkhorn shows a gelatinous layer around an olive embryonic gleba with no gills, while an Amanita button reveals a developing gilled mushroom inside. If any gill structure is present, discard it. If uncertain, do not eat.
distribution: Widespread across Europe and North America, and reported from other temperate regions of the world.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides (Death Cap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: The deadly Death Cap emerges from a white volval egg/button that can resemble a stinkhorn egg. Slice vertically: an Amanita button reveals a developing gilled mushroom (cap, gills, stem), whereas a stinkhorn egg shows a gelatinous layer around an undifferentiated olive embryonic gleba with no gills.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita virosa (Destroying Angel)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly white Amanita whose young volva-enclosed button can be mistaken for a stinkhorn egg. The vertical cut test distinguishes them: gilled mushroom inside = Amanita (discard); gelatinous olive embryo with no gills = stinkhorn.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Mutinus caninus (Dog Stinkhorn)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A related, smaller and more slender stinkhorn that also arises from an egg; harmless but distinguished by its narrower orange-tipped stalk and weaker odor.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Phallus hadriani (Dune Stinkhorn)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A very similar stinkhorn arising from a pinkish/purple-tinged egg, typically in dunes and sandy soils; also edible at the egg stage and not dangerous, but worth distinguishing for accurate ID.

Pleurotus eryngii, the king oyster or king trumpet mushroom, is a choice edible widely cultivated for its thick, meaty white stem and small tan to brown cap. In the wild it grows in association with the roots and decaying tissue of plants in the family Apiaceae, especially Eryngium (sea hollies), giving the species its name.
edibilityNotes: A choice, safe edible that should be cooked before eating; the firm flesh holds its texture well when sauteed, roasted, or grilled. There are no deadly lookalikes within Pleurotus itself, but inexperienced foragers should be aware that the toxic jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus olearius / O. illudens) is sometimes mistaken for oyster-type mushrooms and causes severe gastrointestinal poisoning. Always confirm identification by the decurrent gills, thick central-to-eccentric white stem, and white-to-pale spore print before eating any wild-collected specimen.
habitat: roadsides and disturbed ground where Apiaceae host plants grow
substrate: dead roots and stem bases of Apiaceae
distribution: Native to Mediterranean Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of Central Asia, and now cultivated commercially worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Omphalotus olearius
dangerousLookalikes.note: The toxic jack-o'-lantern has bright orange coloration throughout, true (non-forking) decurrent gills, and grows in clustered tufts on wood or buried roots; it lacks the king oyster's pale meaty stem and tan cap. Causes severe gastrointestinal illness (not deadly, but serious). Omphalotus illudens is the comparable North American species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pleurotus ostreatus
dangerousLookalikes.note: The closely related, also-edible oyster mushroom; distinguished by its broader fan-shaped cap and short or nearly absent lateral stem versus the king oyster's long thick central stem. Not dangerous.

Logs, stumps and standing dead trunks

edibilityNotes: A recognised edible but a poor-quality one: soft-textured, with a mild, sometimes radish-like or earthy flavour, and it does not preserve well. Cook before eating, as with most gilled mushrooms; a small number of reports describe gastric upset, so it is not recommended for the table. There is no well-documented specific raw-toxicity syndrome for this species beyond the general advice to cook wild mushrooms. The dominant safety concern is correct identification: it must be separated from soil-dwelling, pink-spored Entoloma species, several of which are toxic. The combination of a wood-growing habit, truly free gills that mature pink, a salmon-pink (pinkish-brown) spore print, and the complete absence of both a ring and a volva confirms Pluteus rather than Entoloma (which grows from soil/ground and has attached gills). No coprine/alcohol (inkcap) reaction, no puffball or Amanita-egg cut-test, and no muscarine concern apply to this species; those checks belong to other groups and are not relevant here.
description: Pluteus cervinus, the deer shield or fawn mushroom, is a common saprotrophic agaric that fruits on dead and decaying hardwood, including logs, stumps, buried wood, roots, sawdust, and other woody debris. The cap is typically 4-12 cm across, convex becoming flattened, and ranges from grey-brown to dark brown, often with a radially fibrillose or streaky surface and a slightly darker centre. The gills are crowded and truly free from the stem; they start white or pale and mature to a distinctive pink as the spores ripen. The stem is whitish to greyish, fibrillose, and lacks both a ring (partial veil) and a volva (cup at the base). The spore print is salmon-pink to pinkish-brown. Microscopically, the genus Pluteus is characterised by inverse (convergent) hymenophoral trama and prominent cystidia; P. cervinus typically bears thick-walled pleurocystidia with apical hooks or horns. It is one of the few common pink-spored mushrooms that grows directly on wood, which is the key field separator from the soil-dwelling, pink-spored Entoloma.
habitat: on woody debris and wood chips
distribution: Widespread and common in Europe and eastern North America; rare and possibly introduced in western North America. Broadly distributed across the temperate Northern Hemisphere.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Entoloma species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several pink-spored Entoloma species are toxic. Unlike Pluteus cervinus, Entoloma grow from soil/ground (not on wood) and have gills that are attached (adnate to sinuate) rather than free, with angular spores. The wood habitat plus truly free gills distinguish Pluteus. This is the primary dangerous confusion for this species.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Volvariella / Volvopluteus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Also pink-spored with free gills, but these arise from a distinct cup-like volva at the stem base, which Pluteus entirely lacks. Check the stem base before eating any pink-spored, free-gilled mushroom.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Pluteus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Numerous similar wood-growing Pluteus species exist; most require microscopy (cystidia shape) for confident separation. Not a poisoning risk in itself, but it undermines a confident species-level edibility call.

Psilocybe cubensis is a psilocybin-producing mushroom in the family Hymenogastraceae, recognized by its golden-brown to caramel cap, dark purple-brown spore print, and the blue bruising of its flesh where handled. It is a dung-loving (coprophilous) species of warm grasslands and is the most widely cultivated of the "magic mushrooms." This profile is educational/informational only.
edibilityNotes: Contains the controlled psychoactive tryptamines psilocybin and psilocin and is illegal to possess or cultivate in most jurisdictions. Not a culinary food; ingestion produces hallucinogenic effects. Critical safety risk: misidentification with toxic dung- and grass-inhabiting species (e.g. Galerina, Conocybe/Pholiotina) that contain deadly amatoxins. Educational information only — do not consume.
distribution: Pantropical and subtropical, occurring across the Americas (notably the Gulf Coast of the United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America), Southeast Asia, and Australia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: A deadly amatoxin-containing mushroom. It grows on wood/lignin (decaying logs, buried wood) rather than dung, has a rusty-brown (not purple-brown) spore print, and does NOT stain blue. Any brown-spored, non-bluing mushroom in this size class should be treated as potentially deadly.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Conocybe / Pholiotina species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small brown dung- and grass-inhabiting mushrooms; some (e.g. Pholiotina rugosa, formerly Conocybe filaris) contain deadly amatoxins. They have rusty- to cinnamon-brown spore prints, fragile stems, and do not bruise blue.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Panaeolus / other Psilocybe species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Other coprophilous psilocybin and non-psilocybin mushrooms share dung habitat and dark spore prints; precise distinction requires microscopy and spore color, and non-bluing brown-spored species may be toxic.

edibilityNotes: Contains the psychoactive tryptamines psilocybin and psilocin (and minor baeocystin); one of the more potent psilocybin mushrooms by dry-weight concentration. Psilocybin/psilocin are controlled substances in most jurisdictions (e.g. Schedule I in the US, Class A in the UK), so possession, picking, and consumption are illegal in many countries. This is NOT a food mushroom. The greatest practical danger is misidentification: many small brown grassland mushrooms (LBMs) co-occur, and some contain DEADLY amatoxins (Galerina, Pholiotina/Conocybe) that cause delayed-onset (6-24h+) liver and kidney failure. Anyone unable to confidently distinguish these should never consume wild LBMs.
description: Psilocybe semilanceata, the Liberty Cap, is a small psilocybin-containing mushroom widespread in temperate grasslands of the Northern Hemisphere. Its hallmark is a distinctly conical-to-bell-shaped cap with a sharp pointed papilla (nipple) at the apex, typically 5-25 mm across. The cap is hygrophanous, ranging from olive-brown to ochre or buff and drying paler, often with a translucent striate margin and a separable gelatinous pellicle. The stem is slender, sinuous, and long relative to the cap; gills are adnate and darken to purple-brown as the spores mature. The flesh frequently bruises bluish where damaged or with age, reflecting oxidation of psilocin. It is saprotrophic, fruiting in autumn among grasses in nutrient-rich pastures, meadows, lawns, and roadside verges. It grows from decaying grass roots and organic matter in soil, NOT directly on dung, which helps separate it from many coprophilous Panaeolus species. Because it is a small grassland mushroom growing alongside potentially deadly lookalikes, identification demands care.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, especially common in Europe (including the British Isles, where it is one of the most frequent psilocybin species) and parts of North America. Favours cool, moist oceanic and temperate climates.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY amatoxin-containing species. Small brown mushroom with a rusty-brown (not purple-brown) spore print, typically growing on wood/woody debris rather than open grass. Causes delayed-onset (6-24h+) liver and kidney failure that can be fatal. Lacks blue bruising and the sharp pointed papilla of the Liberty Cap.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pholiotina rugosa
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY amatoxin-containing LBM (also treated as Conocybe filaris). Rusty-brown spore print, often with a ring or ring zone on the stem, grows in grass and lawns alongside Liberty Caps. Delayed-onset (6-24h+) amatoxin poisoning causing liver failure. Lacks blue bruising and the conical papillate cap.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Conocybe species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small fragile grassland LBMs with rusty/cinnamon-brown spore prints; some (notably the C. filaris / Pholiotina group) contain DEADLY amatoxins. Conical to bell-shaped but lacking the sharp pointed papilla and blue bruising of the Liberty Cap. Spore-print color (rusty vs purple-brown) is a key separator.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Panaeolus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small dark-spored grassland and dung mushrooms (e.g. Panaeolus foenisecii, P. papilionaceus). Black to very dark spore print and often mottled gills; some grow directly on dung, unlike P. semilanceata. Most are not deadly, but mottled gills, rounded (non-papillate) caps, and dung substrate help separate them; some Panaeolus are themselves psilocybin-active.

Russula emetica, commonly known as The Sickener, is a brittle-fleshed red-capped mushroom of damp conifer woods and Sphagnum bogs. It has a bright scarlet to cherry-red cap (fading to pink or orange with age or weather) whose cuticle peels readily, white to cream gills, a white stem, and a white to yellowish-white spore print. The raw flesh is intensely acrid and peppery. As with many Russula species, the flesh is granular and brittle, snapping like chalk rather than tearing fibrously. It is regarded as toxic: eaten raw or inadequately cooked it causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, colicky cramps), giving rise to its common name. Although some red Russulas are mild and edible, R. emetica's acrid taste and emetic effects mark it as one to avoid; confident identification of the genus to species by colour alone is unreliable, so all acrid red Russulas are best treated with caution.
distribution: Widespread across the Northern Hemisphere in Europe, Asia and North Africa. The extent of its range in North America is uncertain, as many records there refer to related red-capped white-spored species such as Russula silvicola.
edibilityNotes: Toxic when raw or poorly cooked. The raw flesh is intensely acrid and peppery and causes gastrointestinal distress (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, colicky cramps), typically beginning 30 minutes to 3 hours after ingestion. Symptoms are generally short-lived and not life-threatening, but the species should not be eaten. Historically it was parboiled or pickled (which is said to remove the acrid taste and toxins) and eaten in parts of eastern Europe and Russia, but consumption is not recommended. Because many red Russulas look alike and species-level identification by cap colour is unreliable, all acrid red Russulas should be avoided.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Russula nobilis (Beechwood Sickener)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A similarly acrid, toxic red Russula associated with beech; shares the emetic gastrointestinal effects and is easily confused with R. emetica.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Russula sanguinaria (Bloody Brittlegill)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another red, acrid, toxic Russula of conifer woods (often with a reddish flush on the stem); distinguishing red Russulas to species is difficult and several share the acrid, emetic character.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Edible mild red Russulas (e.g. Russula paludosa)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some red-capped Russulas are mild-tasting and edible, but separating them from acrid species like R. emetica requires a careful taste test and microscopy; do not rely on cap colour alone.

edibilityNotes: Toxic. Causes gastrointestinal poisoning (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) usually within a few hours of ingestion; some people also report flushing, sweating, and tingling. Spore exposure can cause irritation of the eyes and respiratory tract (lacrimation, rhinitis, conjunctivitis). Not known to be deadly in healthy adults, but it should never be eaten. The single most important field test: cut any 'puffball' in half before eating. The earthball's interior (gleba) becomes firm and dark purplish-black, often with white marbling, very early, while true edible puffballs (Lycoperdon, Calvatia) are uniformly pure white and homogeneous inside when young. A dark, marbled, or firm interior means do not eat.
description: Scleroderma citrinum, the common earthball or pigskin poison puffball, is a widespread woodland fungus producing roughly globular, stalkless fruiting bodies typically 4-10 cm across. The outer wall (peridium) is thick, tough, and leathery, dull yellow-brown to ochre, and conspicuously cracked into coarse warts or scales giving a 'pigskin' texture. Unlike true puffballs, it lacks a defined apical pore; at maturity the rind splits irregularly to release spores. The defining internal feature is the gleba: firm and marbled blackish-purple (often with fine white veins) even in young specimens, eventually maturing into a dark purple-brown to black spore mass. It attaches to the substrate by a tough root-like base of white mycelial cords. The species is toxic and a notorious cause of mushroom poisoning because of its superficial resemblance to edible puffballs. It has also been reported as an occasional adulterant used to bulk out commercial truffle products, so dark 'truffle' preparations of uncertain origin warrant caution.
distribution: Widespread and common throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including Europe and North America; reported more broadly in temperate regions worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: True puffballs (Lycoperdon species)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible when young, but ONLY while the interior is uniformly pure white and homogeneous. Lycoperdon has a softer, thinner, often spiny-to-granular skin and a clear apical pore. Always cut open: the earthball's firm dark purplish-black marbled gleba is the key distinction.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Giant/large puffballs (Calvatia, Lycoperdon excipuliforme, etc.)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible only with pure white firm flesh inside. The earthball is much harder, has a thick warty rind, and shows a dark marbled interior early. A dark or firm interior always means reject.

dangerousLookalikes.name: True truffles (Tuber species)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Earthball has been reported as an adulterant in dark truffle products. Genuine truffles have characteristic marbled white-veined flesh and a strong aroma; earthball gleba is acrid and the rind is warty and yellow-brown.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Scleroderma species (e.g. Scleroderma verrucosum, Scleroderma areolatum)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Also toxic earthballs; not a safe alternative. All Scleroderma should be treated as inedible/toxic.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Calvatia gigantea
dangerousLookalikes.note: Confusable with Calvatia gigantea (edible). See its profile for how to tell them apart.

Sparassis crispa, the cauliflower mushroom, is a distinctive wood-rotting fungus that forms a large, rounded, cream to pale-yellow rosette composed of many flattened, wavy, ribbon-like lobes, superficially resembling a head of cauliflower or a bath sponge. Fruitbodies arise at the base of conifers (chiefly pines) or from nearby roots, where the fungus causes a brown root and butt rot. The flesh is firm and tough when young, with a pleasant aromatic smell. Specimens can be substantial, commonly 10-40 cm across and weighing up to several kilograms. It is a prized choice edible, but the intricate folds readily trap soil, needles, and insects, so it must be cleaned thoroughly and cooked well before eating.
edibilityNotes: A choice edible when young, firm, and cream-colored. Discard older specimens that have yellowed and toughened. The convoluted lobes trap pine debris and insects, so clean meticulously and cook thoroughly; it is not eaten raw. As with any wild mushroom, eat only a small amount the first time to check personal tolerance, and rely on a verified identification before consuming.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of Europe (e.g. Britain, Scandinavia, Germany, Poland), North America, and Asia, fruiting where suitable conifer (especially pine) hosts occur.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Sparassis spathulata
dangerousLookalikes.note: A closely related cauliflower mushroom with broader, flatter, more erect leaf-like lobes (rather than narrow wavy ribbons), typically at the base of hardwoods such as oak and beech (occasionally pines). Also edible, so confusion is not dangerous, but it is a separate species.

Stropharia rugosoannulata is a large, robust agaric with a wine-red to reddish-brown cap, gills that mature from pale gray to dark purple-brown, and a distinctive thick, wrinkled (rugose), star-fissured ring on the stem. A vigorous wood-chip saprotroph, it is widely cultivated outdoors as a beginner-friendly edible crop.
edibilityNotes: A choice edible that must be thoroughly cooked; raw or undercooked specimens can cause gastrointestinal upset, and some individuals report sensitivity, so try a small portion first. Confirm the dark purple-brown to blackish spore print and the thick, wrinkled, star-fissured ring before eating. The greatest risk to foragers is misidentification: reddish-brown, ringless or cortina-bearing species in genera such as Cortinarius, Galerina, and Pholiotina can superficially resemble it but produce a rust-brown spore print (not purple-brown to black) and may be deadly poisonous (amatoxins/orellanine). Never rely on cap color alone; always verify the spore print color and the rugose, star-shaped ring.
distribution: Found in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere and now widely distributed and cultivated worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Cortinarius species (webcaps)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some toxic webcaps, including deadly orellanine-containing species, can be reddish-brown, but they have a cobweb-like cortina rather than a thick rugose ring, produce a rust-brown spore print (not purple-brown to black), and grow as mycorrhizal partners with trees rather than on wood chips.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Galerina marginata (deadly galerina)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A deadly amatoxin-containing species that fruits on wood and can have a brownish cap and a ring zone, but it is far smaller, has a rust-brown spore print rather than purple-brown to black, and lacks the thick star-fissured rugose ring. Confusion is most likely with young or small Stropharia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Some Agaricus share a ring and dark gills, but they produce a chocolate-brown spore print, lack the wine-red cap and star-fissured rugose ring, and have free gills with a pink young gill stage; a few Agaricus (e.g. yellow-staining group) cause GI upset.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Pholiotina / Conocybe species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small brown ringed LBM-type mushrooms that can occur in mulch and lawns; some (e.g. Pholiotina rugosa) contain deadly amatoxins. They are much smaller, slender, and have a rust-brown spore print, unlike the large robust Stropharia with purple-brown to black spores.

edibilityNotes: Edible and widely gathered. Peel off the slimy glutinous cap pellicle (cuticle) and remove the spongy pore/tube layer before cooking, then cook thoroughly. The slime/pellicle is reported to cause mild gastrointestinal upset (laxative effect, loose stools) in some people if eaten in quantity, raw, or undercooked, and a minority of people experience allergic reactions to the slimy skin. Modest flavor, generally considered inferior to co-occurring boletes. Standard bolete caution applies: only eat a pored mushroom positively identified to species.
description: Suillus luteus, commonly known as Slippery Jack, is an edible bolete in the family Suillaceae. It is recognized by a glutinous, slimy chocolate- to reddish-brown cap that becomes shiny when wet, small yellow pores beneath (rather than gills), and a distinctive membranous partial-veil ring on the upper stem that is often purplish or brownish on its underside. The stem above the ring bears glandular dots. The flesh is whitish to pale yellow and does not stain blue when cut. It is ectomycorrhizal, forming symbiotic associations almost exclusively with pines (Pinus), and is common in pine plantations and forests across the Northern Hemisphere. It has been widely introduced with planted pines into the Southern Hemisphere (e.g. Australia, New Zealand, southern Africa, South America). It is the type species of the genus Suillus.
distribution: Native and widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere (Europe, Asia, North America) in association with pines; widely introduced into the Southern Hemisphere with planted pines.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Paxillus involutus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Brown Roll-rim. A brownish, inrolled-margin mushroom occurring in the same conifer/woodland habitat. Dangerously toxic: repeated consumption can trigger a potentially fatal autoimmune hemolytic reaction, and it also causes acute GI poisoning. It has decurrent gill-like ridges (not true pores) and lacks the slimy cap and stem ring of S. luteus; distinguish by confirming a sponge-like pore layer and the membranous ring.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Suillus granulatus
dangerousLookalikes.note: Similar slimy bolete on pine but lacks a stem ring; young stem apex exudes milky droplets from glandular dots. Edible, so confusion is low-risk, but note the absence of the partial-veil ring that characterizes S. luteus.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Other Suillus species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Several other ringed and ringless Suillus on conifers resemble it; all common Suillus are edible after peeling, so the main risk within the genus is GI upset rather than serious poisoning. Confirm pores (not gills), yellow tubes, and pine association.

Trametes versicolor (Turkey Tail) is an extremely common, cosmopolitan bracket fungus forming thin, leathery, fan-shaped caps with concentric, multicolored zones and a finely velvety upper surface. The underside bears a layer of tiny white pores. It grows in overlapping clusters and rosettes on dead hardwood and is widely used in traditional medicine.
edibilityNotes: Not edible as food: the fruiting body is thin, tough, leathery and indigestible. It is consumed only as a decoction (tea) or as standardized extracts. The polysaccharide-K (PSK/krestin) extract is used as an adjuvant cancer therapy in Japan and PSP is studied in China; do not treat this as general culinary edibility. The mushroom itself is not toxic.
distribution: Cosmopolitan; found throughout temperate forests worldwide, including North America, Europe, and Asia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Stereum ostrea (False Turkey Tail)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous, but commonly confused. Lacks pores: its underside is smooth, not porous. Turkey Tail has a distinct layer of tiny white pores (roughly 3-8 per mm) underneath. Checking for pores is the key ID step before brewing tea.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Trichaptum biforme (Violet-toothed Polypore)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous, but a frequent lookalike. Underside is purplish and toothed/jagged rather than white with fine round pores; the violet tone fades with age but the irregular, toothed hymenophore distinguishes it.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Trametes hirsuta (Hairy Bracket)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous. Coarser, conspicuously hairy grayish-white zones with less vivid coloration; pores generally larger and the surface shaggier.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Trametes ochracea
dangerousLookalikes.note: Not dangerous. Thicker, more bunched zones with browner/ochre tones; less thin and less vividly multicolored than true Turkey Tail.

Tricholoma equestre (Man on Horseback or Yellow Knight) is a medium-sized, fleshy agaric with a yellow to greenish-yellow cap, sulphur-yellow gills, and a pale yellow stem, typically fruiting in autumn on sandy soil in coniferous (especially pine) woodland. The cap is sticky when moist and often becomes finely scaly or fibrillose toward the centre, frequently with adhering sand. The flesh has a mealy (farinaceous) smell and the spore print is white. Long regarded across Europe as a choice edible, it has since the late 1990s/early 2000s been reclassified as toxic: repeated large meals over consecutive days have been linked to delayed-onset rhabdomyolysis (breakdown of skeletal muscle), in some cases progressing to severe muscle pain, dark urine, cardiac and respiratory complications, and death. Because the responsible toxin(s) and toxic dose are not fully characterized and severity appears tied to cumulative consumption, it should not be eaten.
distribution: Widespread across temperate Europe and reported in North America; associated with conifers, particularly pines on sandy soils.
edibilityNotes: Historically prized as a choice edible (often under the synonym Tricholoma flavovirens), but now regarded as toxic. Repeated, large consumption over consecutive days has been associated with delayed-onset rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), with documented serious poisonings and fatalities in Europe. The responsible toxin(s) and a safe threshold are not well characterized. Not recommended for consumption; treat as toxic.

dangerousLookalikes.note: Sulphur Knight; also yellow but has a distinctive unpleasant coal-gas/sulphur smell rather than a mealy odour, and is itself inedible/mildly toxic.

Tricholoma matsutake, the matsutake or pine mushroom, is a choice and highly prized ectomycorrhizal mushroom renowned in Japanese and broader East Asian cuisine. It produces a robust, firm fruitbody with a brown, dry, fibrillose-to-scaly cap that expands from convex to flat, often with the margin remaining inrolled when young. The white, crowded gills are notched (sinuate/adnexed) and attached, and the stout white stipe bears a prominent membranous ring, above which the surface is white and below which it is sheathed with brownish fibrils/scales. The flesh is thick, firm, and white. Its most distinctive feature is a strong, spicy-aromatic odor often described as a mix of cinnamon and sweaty socks. It fruits on the ground in association with pine and other conifers, frequently forming partial rings ("shiro") in well-drained, often nutrient-poor soils. Because of declining harvests and habitat loss, matsutake commands extremely high market prices, and the species has been assessed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.
distribution: East Asia, especially Japan, Korea, and China; also reported from parts of northern Europe and the Nordic region. North American pine mushrooms once attributed to this species are now generally treated under the related taxon Tricholoma murrillianum / the T. magnivelare complex.
edibilityNotes: Choice, highly prized edible valued for its distinctive spicy-aromatic fragrance; typically cooked simply (grilled, in rice, or in clear soup) to preserve the aroma. The critical safety concern is misidentification. In North America especially, the deadly nephrotoxic lookalike Amanita smithiana fruits in the same conifer forests at the same season and at a similar size, and has caused real poisonings among matsutake foragers, producing severe delayed-onset kidney failure (renal injury appearing days after ingestion). Before consuming, always confirm the diagnostic spicy odor, the notched/attached (not free) white gills, and the absence of a volva or bulbous/swollen base. If any of these cannot be confirmed, do not eat.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita smithiana
dangerousLookalikes.note: CRITICAL North American lookalike. Nephrotoxic (allenic norleucine), causing early GI symptoms followed by delayed-onset renal failure days later, often requiring dialysis. Distinguished by free gills (not notched/attached), a swollen/bulbous to rooting base sometimes with volval remnants, and the lack of the matsutake spicy-aromatic odor.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita silvicola
dangerousLookalikes.note: White North American conifer-associated Amanita that can be mistaken for a pale pine mushroom; lacks the matsutake odor and has free gills and a swollen/volval base. Treat as toxic/avoid.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Catathelasma species
dangerousLookalikes.note: Robust pine-associated mushrooms that can superficially resemble matsutake but have decurrent gills and a double ring, and lack the strong spicy matsutake odor. Not the deadly concern, but a common point of confusion.

Volvariella volvacea, the paddy straw mushroom, is a warm-climate species widely cultivated across Southeast and East Asia on rice straw and other plant substrates. It is harvested mostly in its young, egg-like button stage, enclosed in a sac-like volva, and is a major commercial mushroom in tropical regions.
edibilityNotes: Edible and popular when cooked; harvested young in the volva-enclosed "egg" stage. CRITICAL SAFETY WARNING: in its button stage the paddy straw mushroom, enclosed in a basal volva, closely resembles the unexpanded "egg" stage of deadly Amanita species (death cap Amanita phalloides, destroying angels Amanita virosa / A. bisporigera), and such confusion has caused fatal poisonings. Distinguishing features: Volvariella has a PINK to salmon spore print and pink mature gills and NO stem ring (annulus), whereas deadly Amanita have a WHITE spore print, white gills, and usually a ring. Spore print and gill colour are not visible in the unopened button, so wild buttons should never be eaten. Best practice is to rely only on cultivated material; do not gather wild specimens unless an expert confirms identity.
distribution: Native to and cultivated throughout tropical and subtropical Asia, and grown commercially in warm regions worldwide.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides
dangerousLookalikes.note: Death cap; deadly. Has a WHITE spore print, white gills, and a ring (annulus) on the stem. The button/egg stage and volva resemble young Volvariella, but Volvariella has a pink spore print, pink mature gills, and no ring. These features are not visible in the unopened button, so wild buttons must never be eaten.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita virosa
dangerousLookalikes.note: Destroying angel; deadly. White overall with a white spore print, white gills, and a stem ring. Distinguished from paddy straw by Volvariella's pink spore print and gills and the absence of a ring.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita bisporigera
dangerousLookalikes.note: Destroying angel (North American); deadly. All white with a white spore print, white gills, a stem ring, and a basal volva that can mimic a young Volvariella egg. Lacks the pink spores/gills of paddy straw.
